priorities: Safety and production quality through the MAX phase-down. No launch reaches us without Pope's written results on KPIs, suppliers and strain, and she must confirm from the brief, not assume, that no quality, FAA or certification problem is live. MAX output falls from 684 a year in 2044 to 641 in 2045, 428 in 2050 and none in 2060. A line that is winding down must keep its quality KPIs, its fragile suppliers and its trained people, and we want that in writing [BG-0043, BG-0025, BG-0014, B-2330].

Protect the repaired balance sheet and the rating. The risk-case column is now S3 (Airbus Delay Tactics, covert). Do Nothing is -0.28 there, so the floor is -2.28. All 12 fps rows fail it. The best is the 10-year ramp at Renton with the 787 Re-engine at -3.15, short by 0.87. The 10-year at Renton alone is -3.64, short by 1.36. The 787 Re-engine alone passes at +0.46. Net debt stays at $0.0B in the base and stress cases through 2050 on Do Nothing [BG-0029, BG-0062, B-2327].

A business case and a bounded downside before any commitment. A launch must add more than $1B in the expected column, and no item may lose more than $1B in any plausible column. All three columns are plausible: no A350 Re-engine is on the public record, and Delay Tactics are covert. The 787 Re-engine is +0.74 / -0.81 / +0.74, below $1B even in its best column. The cheapest fps launch is -3.31 against Do Nothing [BG-0021, BG-0022, B-0581].

The next airplane comes when the market, the technology and Boeing are ready. Technology is met: the P&W-RR Joint Venture engine has been ready since 2036 and the CFM ducted engine since 2041, so codes 5, 6 and 7 fit two sources at a 2055 EIS. Boeing's cash is met: stress net debt is $0.0B on the 10-year rows. The market leg fails for the third round running, in every column. The fps waits for a grid that carries it, not for NGSA's date [BG-0068, B-2303, B-2313].

One development at a time, and nothing announced ahead of this Board. A 2045 787 Re-engine overlaps a 10-year fps by 2 years, which passes, and a 7-year fps by 5 years, which fails. No public line may present any order as a reply to Airbus [B-2167, B-0438, B-0521].
board_guidance.risk_appetite: Unchanged at 4.5 of 5 on risk aversion and 3 on horizon. We keep the $1B item limit in S1, S2 and S3, and the S3 floor of -2.28. Only hold orders pass on this grid, and we expect to approve Do Nothing.
board_guidance.expect_to_see: (1) The submitted row from the brief's grid. For each Board item, the same row with that field at its default, in S1, S2 and S3. (2) The CEO's expected_scenario, and the risk-case column S3 set against Do Nothing (-0.28; floor -2.28). (3) Malave's buffer test with its numbers and his 'Fundable when the 777X turns' result. Also the stress-case net-debt line from the brief's objective table, which reads: $0.0B for Do Nothing, the Re-engine alone, every 10-year row and the 7-year at Renton alone; $0.7B for the 7-year at new sites; $2.1-3.3B for the 7-year with the Re-engine; $1.6-6.4B for via Embraer. (4) Pope's written results on KPIs, suppliers and two-front strain, confirmed from the brief. These should include the quality and supplier readiness of the MAX line as it winds down (641 a year in 2045, 428 in 2050). For any 787 Re-engine, she should show a widebody engine committed and ready by its 2050 EIS and the amended type certificate before the line converts. (5) The CEO's ruling that H3's second half is in force and not triggered (no A350 Re-engine on the record), and the H4 overlap counts: 0 for the Re-engine alone, 2 beside a 10-year fps, 5 beside a 7-year. (6) Every doctrine or objective premium, logged with its reason against H8's $2B cap. If management holds the Re-engine by its own choice, that is at most $0.74B (S1). (7) A public statement with no fps date and no programme announced ahead of us. It should restate the engine line without naming makers: the 2035 line that 'code 7 fits three sources' is out of date now that GTF2 and UltraFan NB have folded into the Joint Venture. It should name no Airbus move as the reason for any order. Where a piece is missing, we compute it from the brief and say so. A missing piece alone is not a veto ground.
would_approve: fps: hold. It is not a Board item and is never vetoed. The Do Nothing row is -0.28 / -0.61 / -0.28 (S1-S3), and it keeps net debt at $0.0B in the base and stress cases through 2050.
re787: hold. It is not a Board item. It avoids -0.81 in S2 if Airbus re-engines the A350 this round, and gives up at most +0.74 in S1 and S3.
rate_737: hold, the only value the brief offers.

fps_site: new_site (the default), or renton while the fps holds. Either passes: the item value is 0 until a launch. At a launch, Renton adds +0.16 to +0.17 in every column, subject to Pope's readiness result.

fps_engine_code: null while the fps holds. At any launch we would want code 5, 6 or 7, each of which fits CFM plus the P&W-RR Joint Venture (two sources) at a 2055 EIS. The code rides with the launch and is never a veto ground.
would_veto: re787: launch. The item value against Do Nothing is +0.74 / -0.81 / +0.74 (S1-S3). It fails the Business case test: it is below epsilon ($1.00B) in every column, so it fails whichever expected column the CEO names. Weighted with S2 at 20-33%, it is +0.22 to +0.43. Alone it passes the Downside test (-0.81 in S2, inside our -$1B limit). Beside any fps it also fails Downside: -1.06 in S2 beside a 10-year fps; -1.27 beside a 7-year, which also overlaps 5 years; -1.24 beside via Embraer. Its other tests pass alone: S3 +0.46 against the -2.28 floor, stress net debt $0.0B, zero overlap. Alternative: hold.

fps: launch_10yr. Against fps hold the item is -3.47 / -3.47 / -3.53 at new sites and -3.31 / -3.31 / -3.36 at Renton. Beside the Re-engine it is -3.56 to -3.78. It fails Business case, Downside (below -1.0 in every column), Rating first and so Boeing ready. On Rating first, S3 is -3.64 at Renton (short by 1.36) and -3.81 at new sites (short by 1.53); even with the Re-engine it is -3.15 (short by 0.87). Alternative: hold.

fps: launch_7yr. The item is -4.53 to -5.22 at either site, with or without the Re-engine. S3 is -4.59 to -5.05, short of the floor by 2.31-2.77. Stress net debt is $0.7B at new sites, and $2.1-3.3B with the Re-engine, which would also overlap it by 5 years. Its worst column at Renton (-5.14) trails the 10-year ramp's (-3.92) by $1.22B, more than epsilon. Alternative: hold.

fps: launch_via_embraer. The item is -7.35 to -8.00. It is $4.04B worse than the Solo 10-year ramp in every column, so it fails Rating first's Embraer clause. S3 is -7.38 to -7.84, short of the floor by 5.10-5.56, and stress net debt is $1.6-6.4B. The Solo ramps would normally be the named alternatives, but they fail this round too. Alternative: hold.
Plan level: every plan that contains an fps launch fails Rating first in S3. The best, the 10-year at Renton with the Re-engine, is -3.15 against the -2.28 floor. The cure is fps: hold.

recommendations.text: Hold the fps this round. The loss has narrowed but its sign has not changed. The cheapest launch, the 10-year ramp at Renton, was -5.20 against Do Nothing in 2035 and is -3.31 now. Ten years of discounting alone would have brought it to about -1.92, so the growing lag behind NGSA has taken about two-fifths of the relief. On the same trend, a 2050 launch (EIS 2057 or 2060) would sit at roughly -2.0 to -2.6 (our inference). That is still short of the +$1B business case and our -$1B limit. When an fps comes, it should come Solo on the 10-year ramp: its worst column beats the 7-year's by $1.22B and its bill is smaller. It should come at Renton (+0.16 to +0.17), with code 5, 6 or 7. No date in public before launch, and a conservative EIS at launch.

On the 787 Re-engine, we speak plainly. On this grid we would veto it on the Business case: +0.74 in its best columns is below epsilon, and -0.81 if the A350 re-engines. Beside any fps it also breaches our Downside limit (-1.06 to -1.27). As Malave forecast in 2035, the window closed with that round. Unless a later grid shows more than $1B in the expected column, we regard the file as closed on its numbers, not because of any Airbus move. If management holds it by its own choice, log the value given up (at most $0.74B in S1) as a premium within H8. If we veto it, the value is our constraint. If the A350 re-engines, H3's second half closes the question for good. Keep the 787 and 777X lines stable: the 58.8% widebody position holds on the status-quo path.

Bring the engine-source line up to date. GTF2 and UltraFan NB have folded into the P&W-RR Joint Venture, which formed in 2035 and has been ready since 2036. At a 2055 EIS, codes 5, 6 and 7 each fit two sources (CFM and the Joint Venture), and code 4 fits one. The 2035 public line that code 7 'fits three sources' no longer holds, so restate the requirement as 'more than one engine source' and name no maker. Three narrowbody engine makers stay in the market in 2045 and 2050. Keep the second-source talks private. Pope should confirm Joint Venture capacity and durability, given P&W's open GTF fleet work, before any code is chosen.

The Aerospace Safety Committee asks for written assurance on the MAX phase-down. Volumes fall from 684 in 2044 to 641 in 2045 and 428 in 2050, and reach none by 2060. A shrinking line loses people and suppliers, and that is a quality risk before it is a cost. We want Pope's KPI results for the tail, fragile suppliers funded and hot, LEAP-1B and materials secured for our own lines, and support for the in-service fleet kept whole. Weekly safety-review risks should keep reaching us. Any plan must have no production-certification concurrency and no fixed-price development.

We are a long-cycle business, and 2050 is the last round. Bring us a written, honest franchise view now. It should cover two things. First, the 2050 grid's best Solo 10-year launch set against Do Nothing on our tests. Second, if that fails, the plan for the narrowbody tail and for the widebody and services base that carries the company beyond it. Preference on Do Nothing falls from 31% in 2045 to 26% in 2050. At horizon 3 we grant no extra downside for a long-term position, and we will not approve a launch at a loss beyond our limits to defend a share objective. A decline honestly reported is better than an unfunded promise. Keep the option warm at no cost on the grid: workforce, suppliers, engines and the Renton plan.

The public statement and the package. The statement should give no fps date, announce no programme ahead of this Board, and present no Airbus move as the reason for any order. Rates stay KPI-gated and agreed with the FAA. Say nothing on returning cash to the owners. Net debt is $0 in the base and stress cases through 2050, but that question is reserved to this Board, and we will take it up ourselves. In the package, show the following: the submitted row and each item row across S1-S3; S3 against Do Nothing (floor -2.28); Malave's buffer, stress net-debt and Fundable results; Pope's KPI, supplier and strain results in writing; the status of H3's second half and the H4 overlap counts; and every premium logged against H8's $2B cap.

frame.question:
It's 2045, the third of four rounds. NGSA has been in service for eight years. Our narrowbody preference is 31% and falls about a point a year, and the 737 MAX has started its phase-down: 641 a year in 2045, 428 in 2050, none in 2060. Two questions.

(1) Does anything on this grid clear the bar?
- fps: this is the third test of the three work streams. Technology is met: the P&W-RR Joint Venture engine has been ready since 2036 and the CFM ducted engine since 2041. Boeing is met: net debt is $0 in the base and stress cases. Is the market met? Does any fps row beat Do Nothing by more than epsilon and pass Malave's buffer?
- 787 Re-engine: is this its last window, and does it clear epsilon at all?

(2) If nothing clears, what is the honest plan into 2050, the last round? My working answer:
- hold now, and keep the fps option warm at no cost on the grid;
- keep the MAX tail safe and stable as it winds down;
- bring the Board a written franchise view: what the 2050 grid would have to show, and what we do if it doesn't.
frame.situation:
PUBLIC RECORD (2045 bulletin)
- NGSA has been in service since 2037 with CFM, PW and RR (code 7), on the Alt plan. Airbus says A320 lines run longer through the ramp, 'rate by rate, quality first'.
- 2035 engine moves:
  - P&W and Rolls-Royce both committed to the Joint Venture. GTF2 and UltraFan NB folded into it, and the Joint Venture engine has been ready since 2036.
  - The CFM ducted engine launched in 2035 and has been ready since 2041.
  - The CFM-Embraer partnership has been ready since 2042.
  - The GEnx upgrade has been ready since 2033.
- No A350 Re-engine is on the record, and Rolls-Royce has launched no widebody engine.
- Our 2035 orders were Do Nothing, with no Board items. Our 2035 public line said code 7 fits three sources. That is out of date now that GTF2 and UltraFan NB have folded into the Joint Venture, and I will correct it [BX-1284].
- Observed in 2044: NB delivered share 30.4% (569 against Airbus's 1,108). Capacity bound in 2039-43, with 225-402 customers waiting. WB share 58.8%. NB engines CFM 51.8%, P&W 24.1%, RR 24.1%.

OUR POSITION (brief section 1)
- Do Nothing is -0.28 against the status quo: NB operating profit -3.64, supply and demand +3.36.
- The status quo also phases out the MAX by 2060, so the narrowbody run-down is in both baselines.
- Preference: 31% (2045), 29% (2047), 26% (2050), 21% (2055), 16% (2060). Delivered share: 27.6% (2045), 22.1% (2050), 0% (2060).
- MAX capacity against what customers want from us:
  - 2045-47: we are demand-limited. Capacity 641 against 511 delivered (130 slots idle); in 2047, 556 against 482.
  - From 2050 the phase-out binds: customers want 437 against 428 of capacity; 365 against 299 in 2053; 305 against 214 in 2055.
- Operating profit: 5.6 in 2045 (status quo 6.1), 5.2 in 2050, and 3.6 in 2060, which is widebody only.
- Net debt is $0.0B in base and stress through 2060 on Do Nothing.

OBJECTIVES (brief section 2)
- Not met:
  - 50/50 split and incumbency (worst year 26%).
  - Dual sources on our NB in production. The MAX flies CFM only, and no fps launched now can be in production by 2050: a 7-year launch enters service in 2052.
- Met: repair (2029), kept repaired in base and stress, and three NB engine makers in 2045 and 2050.

KPIs
- The brief reports no quality, FAA, certification or supply-chain problem.
- The FAA-process gate passes, and H7 has no trigger.
- The only rate value offered is hold.

ENGINE CODES at a 2055 EIS
- Codes 5, 6 and 7: CFM + Joint Venture, two sources.
- Codes 1, 2 and 4: the Joint Venture alone, one source.
- Code 3: CFM alone, one source.

GRID (S1 rivals hold; S2 Airbus launches the A350 Re-engine; S3 risk case, covert Delay Tactics)
- Do Nothing: -0.28 / -0.61 / -0.28. Malave's floor in S3 is -2.28.
- Re-engine alone: +0.46 / -1.42 / +0.46. The item is +0.74 / -0.81 / +0.74, below epsilon in every column.
- All 12 fps rows fail the floor:
  - the best is the 10-year at Renton with the Re-engine, -3.15, short by 0.87;
  - the cheapest launch, the 10-year at Renton, is -3.31 / -3.31 / -3.36 against Do Nothing.
- S3 moves the fps rows by only 0.05-0.06 against S1. The fps fails on its own numbers, not on anything Airbus does.
- Trend on the cheapest launch: -5.20 in 2035, -3.31 now. Ten years of discounting alone would have given -1.92, so the growing lag behind NGSA took about two-fifths of the relief.

BOARD GUIDANCE (non-binding; its veto comes after my decision)
- Risk aversion 4.5 of 5. It expects to approve Do Nothing.
- Would veto:
  - re787: launch, on the Business case: below epsilon in every column, and beside any fps -1.06 to -1.27 in S2;
  - every fps launch, on Business case, Downside and Rating first;

  - Malave's buffer, stress net-debt and 'Fundable when the 777X turns' results;
  - my H3 and H4 rulings;
  - every premium logged;
  - the engine line restated without makers;
  - an honest franchise view before 2050.

(2) For the Board, each item row in S1-S3 against the same row with that field at its default:

- the Re-engine beside a 10-year fps: +0.49 / -1.06 / +0.49;
- beside a 7-year: +0.28 / -1.27 / +0.29;

(5) Cash timing on the standard curve, and your 'Fundable when the 777X turns' result for each:

- fps 10-year: $60.32B over 2045-54, booked at 2055;
- fps 7-year: $65.00B over 2045-51, booked at 2052.

(6) Slip leg, one conservative reset [BX-1318, BX-1319]:

- the 10-year fps with two years added (EIS 2057): how much further below Do Nothing does D or C fall?

(7) Your number for a same-round A350 Re-engine (S2), with reasons both ways. The Re-engine item is below epsilon at any probability, so your number does not decide the order. It sizes the premium and sets my expected column.

(8) The cost of waiting on the fps. This is the question I most want answered.

frame.initial_lean:
We're not ready for a new airplane on this grid, and I'm not going to pretend we are. I also want to be plain about what that means [BX-1286, BX-1300].

fps: HOLD (code null, new_site).

  - technology: CFM plus the Joint Venture gives two sources at a 2055 EIS;

re787: HOLD.

FRANCHISE VIEW, in draft for the Board. This is the hard part, and I'll say it straight.
- On this board the MAX is gone by 2060 whatever we order, in the status quo too.
- Customers want 437 a year from us in 2050 and 305 in 2055.
- An fps 18 years behind NGSA, into a market that shrinks after the mid-2050s with COMAC and a new entrant taking the top, does not pay its bill in any column.
- Waiting has narrowed the loss, from -5.20 to -3.31, but has not changed its sign. Holding now looks cheaper than launching now even on a path where we launch in 2050 (Malave to confirm).
- So we decide the fps on the 2050 grid against the same bar, and keep the option warm at no cost: workforce, suppliers, engines, the Renton plan.
- If 2050 fails too, the honest plan is a safe, stable narrowbody tail and a company carried by the widebody and services.
- 'while doing the first 3, we must build a new future for Boeing' [BX-1245]. I haven't found one this grid will fund, and I'd rather report a decline honestly than book a promise I can't pay for.

MAX TAIL. This is the priority this round: safety and quality over efficiency [BX-1294], stability over share [BX-1274]. I want Pope's written assurance in the package.

What would change my lean:
- a grid error Malave finds;
- evidence from Pope that a 2045 launch is the last one operations can hand over warm, and that a 2050 launch would cost more than the grid shows. Even then, the buffer veto binds on every fps row this round.

BOARD RISK: the Board would veto re787: launch and every fps launch. My lean carries no Board item, so I expect approval.

PUBLIC LINE:

cfo.memo:
Kelly, I ran every row with the risk case, S3, as the baseline: Do Nothing -0.28, floor -2.28. Your numbers check.

fps: all twelve rows fail, so my veto stands on every launch, and the team rule makes it binding. The closest, the 10-year at Renton with the Re-engine, is -3.15, $0.87B short; the 10-year at Renton alone is $1.36B short. Funding isn't the gate: the 777X turned in 2029 and stress net debt holds at $0.0B. The market is.

Waiting is the cheaper path. On the trend, a 2050 Solo 10-year sits near -2.2 against Do Nothing, the 7-year near -3.1. Holding now beats launching now by about $1.1B even if we launch in 2050, and by $3.31B if we never do. The business case would still need a swing of about $3B, barring a market after 2060 that holds up rather than falling with replacement.

Re-engine: it clears my buffer at +0.46, so no veto from me. But the item is +0.74 at best, below epsilon at any probability, and I put a same-round A350 move at about one in five. On a tie I take the better worst column, -0.61 against -1.42. Hold; the premium is $0.74B on S1, $0.43B on my column.

Franchise: narrowbody profit runs to zero by 2060 and the widebody carries $3.6B a year. Net debt stays at zero; the stress case covers the run-down in full.

While disappointing, hold is the higher-confidence plan, and we keep the option warm.

Every hit is either a statement of principle or a move a rival made for its own lines: our 2035 line ('Our KPIs are stable', 57 a month); Airbus's 'rate by rate, quality first' and its quality-gated A320-to-NGSA pacing; CFM's 'safety, quality, delivery and cost' and its supply priority (fleet kits and spares first, 'spares never crowding out OE', lean before capital at its constrained suppliers). None of them reports a Boeing quality, FAA, certification or supply-chain problem. tests.name: MAX phase-down assurance for the Aerospace Safety Committee (doctrine; the rate-down discipline is my inference). Answers CEO ask 2
tests.threshold: Written assurance, confirmed from the brief: (a) quality KPIs held on a shrinking line; (b) fragile suppliers funded and hot; (c) LEAP-1B and materials secured; (d) trained people kept; (e) in-service fleet supported in full; (f) a plain rule for the last customers once capacity binds. Rate-downs are taken like rate-ups: one step at a time, KPI-gated, with no other change stacked on a rate break
tests.numbers:
The brief reports no problem (test 1). The glide path, from the brief: deliveries 511 (2045, 42.6 a month), 508, 482, 472, 469 (2049, 39.1 a month). From 2050 capacity binds: 428 (35.7 a month), 385, 342, 299 (2053, 24.9), 256, 214 (2055, 17.8), 171, 128, 86, 43, 0 (2060). Capacity falls about 43 a year, or 3.6 a month, which is less than one 5-a-month step a year.
(a) Quality. The line already fell from 57 a month (684 in 2043) to 47.4 (569 in 2044), and goes to 42.6 in 2045. Plan the build to deliveries, not to capacity. Idle slots are 130 (2045), 90, 74, 41 and 1 (2049), so 2045-49 is a stable plateau of 39-43 a month, a drift of 3.5 a month over four years. From 2050, take one step-down at a time and hold its KPIs before the next. Consolidate lines one at a time, never during a rate break [B-1446]. By 2056 the tail (14.2 a month) fits on one 15-a-month line (inference).
(b) Suppliers. Volume against 2043 is down 25% (2045), 37% (2050) and 69% (2055). Fund the fragile suppliers and keep them paced with buffers [B-2330, BX-1243, B-2043]. Where a supplier exits, plan last-time buys and keep its tooling for spares.
(c) LEAP-1B. Original-equipment demand is 2 engines per aircraft: 1,022 engines (2045), 856 (2050) and 428 (2055), plus fleet spares. CFM's public rule protects original equipment ('spares never crowding out OE'), but the LEAP-1B becomes a falling line behind CFM's Ducted work. Secure tail volumes and spares privately now. Materials are for our own lines only and are attributed to no one.
(d) People. Hiring, transfers and retention [B-1941, B-0729, B-1835]. Widebody output is flat at 100 a year, so it cannot absorb the tail workforce. Keep the core team on fps design maturation.
(e) Fleet. The board delivers 15,746 MAX in 2026-59 (10,952 by 2044 and 4,794 more). Support stays whole for the fleet's life. That is a services commitment, not priced on the board [BX-1273, BX-1331].
(f) Last customers. From 2050 customers want 437 against 428 (9 short), 365 against 299 in 2053 (66 short), 305 against 214 in 2055 (91 short), and 137 against 0 in 2060. Tell them plainly and early. Serve firm orders first, then waiting customers in sequence. Promise nothing beyond the glide path, and do not stretch the line [BX-1274]. Report risks weekly to the Aerospace Safety Committee [BG-0043].
Limit: the board carries no KPI, supplier or workforce data, so this is a plan with triggers, not a measurement

ops.memo:
My seat runs mostly on Boeing's operations doctrine; my own record is Global Services, and I say so. Three results, in order.

First and foremost, on-time predictable delivery. I searched the 2045 brief: it reports no quality, FAA, certification or supply-chain problem, and only hold is offered, so my KPI veto has nothing to bind on. The MAX tail is a known glide path. We deliver 511 in 2045 against 641 of capacity, so we plan the line to 43 a month, not 53. It holds 39-43 a month through 2049, then steps down about 3.6 a month each year, one KPI-gated step at a time. Fragile suppliers funded, LEAP-1B and spares secured, the fleet supported whole, and the last customers told plainly: 305 want us in 2055 against 214 built. This is a plan with triggers, not a measured KPI; the board carries none. And '57 a month' leaves the public line.

Second, engineering capacity. Re-engine alone: zero overlap. Beside a 10-year fps or via Embraer: 2 years, $1.2B. Beside a 7-year: 5 years, $3.0B, an H4 breach. Operations can deliver the Re-engine, but +0.74 is below epsilon: hold.

And finally, disciplined profitable growth. Hold the fps: it fails on value, not on date. Via Embraer costs $4.04B more and adds nothing we lack. Yes, 2045 is the last warm handover. But a cold one would have to cost $13-39B in 2055-60 money to beat waiting. Sensitivity: every 10 MAX a year is about $0.04B of profit.

decision.public_statement:
Ten years ago we said we'd get the basics right first, and we have. The balance sheet is where we said we'd put it, and it has stayed there. The 777X and the 737-7 and -10 are in service, and the 787 and 777X lines are stable.

First, a correction. Last time I said the 737 line was steady at 57 a month. That number is behind us now, and I'd rather fix it than leave it out there. The 737 MAX is in the later part of its life. We'll build it at the pace our customers need, and we'll step it down the same way we stepped it up: one step at a time, on the data, agreed with the FAA. Quality comes ahead of the schedule on the way down, just as it did on the way up. And every MAX in service will have our full support for as long as it flies.

On a new single-aisle airplane, how we decide hasn't changed. We look at three things: the market, the technology and our own readiness. The technology is there, and so is our balance sheet. The business case isn't, and I'm not going to launch an airplane until it is. I'm not going to give you a date, and I'd rather tell you that plainly than sell you a promise I can't keep.

One more correction, on engines. When we do launch, the airplane will carry more than one engine source, from engines that are ready when the airplane is. That's the requirement. I'm not going to name makers today, and the entry-into-service date will have headroom built in.

In the meantime we're keeping our engineering team and our supply base ready, so that when the time is right we can execute. It is so much more important that we do this right than fast.
decision.rationale:
DECISION. I order Do Nothing, the row 'fps: hold + 787: hold': -0.28 / -0.61 / -0.28 (S1-S3).
- fps hold, code null, rate_737 hold, re787 hold, fps_site new_site.
- Every order is the default, so nothing goes to the Board for approval. The full case still goes with the package [BG-0022].
- I checked the grid against the brief myself. Weighted columns and break-evens are in /tmp/wargame-boeing/dash-2050-phaseout/work/r3_calc.txt.

TEAM RULE.

final.public_statement:
Ten years ago we said we'd get the basics right first, and we have. The balance sheet is where we said we'd put it, and it has stayed there. The 777X and the 737-7 and -10 are in service, and the 787 and 777X lines are stable.

First, a correction. Last time I said the 737 line was steady at 57 a month. That number is behind us now, and I'd rather fix it than leave it out there. The 737 MAX is in the later part of its life. We'll build it at the pace our customers need, and we'll step it down the same way we stepped it up: one step at a time, on the data, agreed with the FAA. Quality comes ahead of the schedule on the way down, just as it did on the way up. And every MAX in service will have our full support for as long as it flies.

On a new single-aisle airplane, how we decide hasn't changed. We look at three things: the market, the technology and our own readiness. The technology is there, and so is our balance sheet. The business case isn't, and I'm not going to launch an airplane until it is. I'm not going to give you a date, and I'd rather tell you that plainly than sell you a promise I can't keep.

One more correction, on engines. When we do launch, the airplane will carry more than one engine source, from engines that are ready when the airplane is. That's the requirement. I'm not going to name makers today, and the entry-into-service date will have headroom built in.

In the meantime we're keeping our engineering team and our supply base ready, so that when the time is right we can execute. It is so much more important that we do this right than fast.

The A350 Re-engine. In rounds 1 and 2 the Board named the 2045 round as the earliest clean start, provided no 787 Re-engine was on the record and that round's grid passed its tests. Both conditions now hold.
- Liquidity: $1.0B a year with no strain, against $5.23B.

- if Boeing launches a 787 Re-engine this round, rule 3 closes the A350 Re-engine for good;

That is short of the $1B that both the ExCo's rule and the Board's override review require. The Board would veto an override-carried Re-engine on the governance ground, and the game's one override should stay in reserve.

Keep Delay Tactics at none. With no fps on the record, every move is naked (one move: -11.45 in S1, -11.46 in S6), and it gains at most +0.22 in any fps column. - Each payout should be proposed inside the 30-50% policy.

Public statement. The round-2 line ('the programme remains in development ... second half of the 2030s') should give way to NGSA in service and the ramp 'rate by rate, quality first'. Mr Wagner should report the maturity of the Joint Venture engine and of CFM's new ducted engine, and certify any new standard in sequence without dropping CFM. Any write-off ($5B x years elapsed / 5) would be booked as a charge in reported EBIT, not hidden in the adjusted figure.

tests.name: Five pillars, internal control and disclosure
tests.threshold: No order or statement whose integrity or compliance I could not defend to the Audit Committee; the Board vets all market disclosures; no internal targets
tests.numbers:
Nothing in the default package is covert, and every spend is on the record. 'Funded within our cash flow' holds on either path ($0 or $1.0B against $5.23B).

The round-2 public line ('remains in development ... second half of the 2030s') is out of date and must give way to NGSA in service. Only Board-approved text is published [AX-0004]. It carries no internal targets [AX-0005], no word of Delay Tactics and no state money.

Supply security and the talent programme remain first claims on our own needs, not bottleneck or poaching.

tests.name: Engine code
tests.threshold: No financial test; defer to Mr Wagner on supply
tests.numbers: NGSA is in service, so under the rules its code can no longer change, and it has no payoff effect. It is null in my orders, and I defer to Mr Wagner. The objective counts two sources (CFM and the Joint Venture) and three makers in 2045 and 2050 on every row.

vetoes.plan: NGSA hold (A320 Alt plan) + A350 Re-engine launched in 2045 (rea350: launch), on its own or with Delay Tactics
vetoes.ground:
Soft veto: the added item fails the robustness test.

Against the same plan without it, the item is +0.89 / +0.89 / +0.89 / +0.89 / +0.89 / -0.51 / -0.50. It is negative in S6-S7, which the bulletin does not rule out, and short of $1B in every column (profile §6; the drafter's reading).

Margin against the best passing option (hold, the default): +0.89 at best, +0.75 on the CEO's weights, and -0.51 in the worst column. That is under $1B in every column, so the team rule offers no override route, and the Board would veto an override-carried item.

This is not a red line: peak cash ($1.0B against $5.228B), rule 3 (open) and rule 6 (one launch, 0 years of overlap) all pass. Whether to override is the CEO's call, not mine to pre-clear; on these numbers the rule does not allow it. With Delay Tactics added, the row also breaks rule 4 (see below).

vetoes.plan: Every Delay Tactics row: bottleneck, poaching or both, on hold or with an A350 Re-engine
vetoes.ground:
Company red lines, not overridable.

Rule 4: no fps is on the record, so every move is naked and draws the $48.32B fine, booked in 2045. That is $11.20B in PV, 9.2 years of free cash flow, and 2.3-3.9 times my stress net cash. One move is -11.45 in S1 and -11.46 in S6, and at most +0.22 (S4) anywhere. It falls short of $1B in every column and breaks the Board's $2B loss limit in S1 and S6. `both` is a second move that buys nothing (-0.19 to -0.27).

Rule 5: on the hold row nothing is in development, so poaching has no programme to serve.

The Board vetoes all three this round. The team's stricter condition stands.

cfo.would_change_mind_if:
I would change my view if any of the following is shown:

(1) The public record rules out S6-S7, so that no 787 Re-engine is plausible this round. The item would then be +0.89 in every plausible column, my robustness test would pass, and I would lift the soft veto. Cash already passes. Whether +0.89 is enough under the company's $1B doctrine would then be the CEO's call, not a CFO veto.

(2) A grid shows the A350 Re-engine at least $1B over hold in the expected column.

(3) The Board decides otherwise.

(4) Audited net cash at the start of 2045 comes in well below my stress low case ($12.5B), or FCF falls well below the 2025 base. I would then recalibrate the payout toward the policy floor and hold any discretionary buyback. This would not change the orders: on flat cash, the Re-engine path adds cash at any payout up to 74%.

(5) The extra lines or the Alt tail carry a reported cost of more than about $4.1B in a single year, counted as programme spend. That would test the line on the Re-engine path.
cfo.memo:
Test memo to the CEO and the Board, round 3 (2045). I concur with the lean: ngsa hold, rea350 hold, delay_tactics none, a320_plan alt. No engine code: NGSA is in service; the field is Mr Wagner's. No Board item.

Peak cash. NGSA's cash years ended in 2036. An A350 Re-engine costs $5B / 5 = $1.0B a year in 2045-2049, with no strain, against one year's free cash flow: EUR 4,753m x 1.10 = $5.228B [AX-0104]. Pass: $4.23B of headroom. The extra lines also run in the status quo and sit in industrial capex.

Balance sheet. The brief carries none. On my round-2 flat-cash stress, net cash enters 2045 at $12.5-21.4B; the Re-engine path still adds $1.36-1.47B a year at a 48-50% payout. I propose 48%. Renew the 18-month, 10% authority for share-plan cover; a discretionary programme needs audited net cash. No equity raise, no state money.

Robustness. Both rows are positive everywhere: default worst S4 +10.83, Re-engine row worst S7 +10.93. The item is not: +0.89 in S1-S5, -0.51 / -0.50 in S6-S7, +0.75 weighted. It turns negative in a plausible column and misses $1B everywhere. Soft veto, binding; no override can carry +0.89. Not a red line: cash, rule 3 and rule 6 pass.

Forgone: +0.89 in S1. A 2050 launch is worth at most about +0.6; holding closes the window in practice.

Delay Tactics: red line. Naked; the $48.32B fine is 9.2 years of free cash flow.

A prudent risk approach [AX-0022].

tests.name: Safety, quality and the five pillars: the package and the public line (asks 1 and 7)
tests.threshold: No order, and no public explanation, that contradicts safety and quality. No rate step goes ahead of its quality KPIs, and no quality is traded for the 60/40 objective.
tests.numbers:
- The brief reports no safety, quality or supply event on NGSA (in service since 2037), the A320 tail or the A350 and A350F.
- Every order in the lean is a default, and none is covert.

Public line (ask 7), confirmed:
- NGSA is 'in service'. The round-2 line ('remains in development ... second half of the 2030s') is now out of date.
- The ramp is 'rate by rate, quality first'.
- No rate-100 or extra-line figure goes out. Those are internal operating plan.
- No supplier is named and no past reset is mentioned. If the A350 is held, no engine maker is named as the reason.
- Windows, not dates, for any Re-engine.
- No word of Delay Tactics.

tests.name: The NGSA ramp to about rate 100 and the extra lines, each step gated on quality KPIs (ask 2)
tests.threshold: Each NGSA rate step, and each extra-line step (5 a month more each year, up to 20), goes ahead only once its quality KPIs are met. No step is taken to improve the objective.
tests.numbers:
Capacity against deliveries (brief):
- 2044: 175 + 1,143 = 1,318 against 1,108. Slack 210.
- 2045: 26 + 1,302 = 1,328 (about 111 a month, of which about 108.5 NGSA) against 1,137 (about 95 a month). Slack 191; 85.6% used.
- 2047: 1,429 (about 119 a month) against 1,180 (about 98). Slack 249; 82.6% used.
- 2050: 1,489 (about 124 a month) against 1,250 (about 104). Slack 239; 83.9% used.
There is no waiting backlog in any of these years.

On the brief's numbers the extra lines are not needed to meet demand in 2045-2050. A step that misses its KPIs can wait without losing a delivery.

Gates for every step (inference; the brief gives no thresholds):
1. Conformance and concessions at the current rate held flat or improving, with zero safety-related escapes.
2. Engines (CFM and the Joint Venture) and work packages on time for the next rate, with no draw on fleet spares, and titanium and rare earths covered.
3. Staffing for the next rate from recruitment and internal development, trained before the step.

I hold no step back today, because no event is reported. Objective preference reads 69.0% in 2045 and 74.0% in 2050, so pushing a step gains nothing.

tests.name: The last A320s, the LEAP-1A and GTF tail supply, and closing out the 2038-2041 pacing measure (ask 3)
tests.threshold: Tail engines contracted without drawing on fleet spares. The A320 line's own KPIs hold. The A320 never builds above 82 a month after NGSA entered service.
tests.numbers:
A320 capacity:
- 175 in 2044, 26 in 2045, 0 by 2047. 2046 is not shown in the brief.
- 26 aircraft need 52 engines: about 31 LEAP-1A and 21 GTF on the board's 60/40 split.

Tail supply:
- The public record holds it 'to about 2045' (round-2 move). The brief reports no further status and no supplier refusal.
- 2045 is covered at the edge of that window. Any unit built in 2046 needs its engines confirmed before build, without fleet spares. I report this to the Board's safety review.
- Watch item, as attribution: P&W says 'GTF fleet first', and CFM puts fleet kits and spares ahead of new development ('spares never crowding out OE').

Pacing measure:
- Its period was capacity-bound: 2039 827/827, 2040 852/852, 2041 1,077 against 1,076, 2042 1,129 against 1,128, 2043 1,172 against 1,173.
- From 2044 the line is demand-bound: 1,108 delivered against 1,318 of capacity.
- The period is over and the brief reports no event. I recommend closing the measure at the safety review.
- The brief carries no KPI detail, so the close-out reports 'no safety, quality or supply event recorded' and claims no figure.

tests.name: Supply crunch (ask 4)
tests.threshold: If the brief reports a supply-chain crunch, no new concurrency.
tests.numbers:
- None is reported: nothing on engines, work packages, titanium or rare earths.
- Engine volume: about 2,274 new-type and A320 engines in 2045 (1,137 aircraft) and about 2,500 in 2050 (1,250), from CFM and the Joint Venture.
- No engine maker publishes a capacity figure (CFM: none published), and the brief reports no shortfall.
- Supply security for our own work packages, titanium and rare earths has been renewed on the record. It is a first claim on our own needs only.
- An A350 Re-engine would add a new widebody engine on a line of 70 a year (brief). On the brief's numbers that volume creates no crunch.

tests.name: Engine supply and maturity on NGSA (ask 4; code recommendation, not a veto ground)
tests.threshold: CFM plus at least one second maker. Any new engine standard is certified in sequence, never dropping CFM.
tests.numbers:
- The code is final because NGSA is in service.
- Fitted: CFM + P&W + RR. That is 2 sources (CFM and the Joint Venture) and 3 makers in 2045 and 2050 on every row.

Joint Venture engine:
- Ready since 2036 and on NGSA since 2037.
- Narrowbody engine share: RR rose from 0.2% (2037) to 24.1% (2044); P&W was 24.1% in 2044.
- About eight years in service at rising volume.

CFM ducted engine:
- Ready since 2041, four years ago. CFM's own line puts durability ahead of dates.
- Certify it on NGSA in sequence. Cut it in only at a rate step whose KPIs are met, and keep the current CFM standard until then.

No maturity slip is reported.

tests.name: Engineering capacity: A350 Re-engine launched in 2045 (ask 5a; rule 6)
tests.threshold: NGSA and A350 Re-engine development may overlap by 2 years or less ($1.2B strain) unless the grid shows at least $1B more. At most one new launch per round.
tests.numbers:
- NGSA development ran 2030-2036 and has ended. A350 Re-engine development would run 2045-2049.
- Overlap: 0 years. Strain: $3B x 0/5 = $0. It would be the only launch this round.
- Staffing must come from recruitment and internal development (the renewed talent programme), not from the NGSA ramp.

Operating flag, not a failed test: those development years run alongside NGSA capacity rising from 1,302 to 1,489 and five extra-line steps. The same production-engineering, quality and supplier-development people serve both. The 191-249 aircraft of slack keeps this manageable.

tests.name: A350F and Spirit A350 absorption (ask 5c)
tests.threshold: No A350 Re-engine while the A350F and the Spirit A350 work packages are being absorbed. Game proxy: round 2 at the earliest.
tests.numbers:
- 2045 is round 3.
- The A350F entered its industrial phase in 2025, and the Spirit packages date from 2025-26. The brief reports nothing on either, so treating both as absorbed is an inference.
- The A350 line runs flat at 70 widebody deliveries a year (41.2%). An entry into service in 2050 would cut a new engine into a steady line.

tests.name: A350 Re-engine: engine readiness for entry into service in 2050 (ask 5b; teams.md Step 3 engine test, inference)
tests.threshold: Step 3 passes the default engine (Rolls-Royce on the A350) when it adds no years. Any other engine, or one that adds years, needs at least $1B on the grid. Faury's own condition: no derivative on an engine that is not ready by its entry into service.
tests.numbers:
The default maker:
- The A350 flies Rolls-Royce Trent XWB, and our widebodies fly Rolls-Royce only.
- The public record shows no UltraFan widebody launch and no other new widebody engine for the A350.
- Under rules.md the UltraFan widebody is ready 6 years after launch. Launched this round it is ready in 2051, one year after a 2050 entry into service; launched in 2050, it is ready in 2056.
- The Trent 1000 upgrade is a 787 engine.

The only mature alternative:
- The GEnx upgrade, ready since 2033, is GE's 787 engine. It has never been fitted to the A350, and no GE offer for the A350 is on the record.
- So a mature engine exists for 2050 only from a non-default maker, as a new integration.

Against the grid:
- Item: +0.89 in S1-S5, -0.51 / -0.50 in S6-S7, +0.75 on Faury's weights.
- Below $1B in every column, so it fails.

Caveat:
- The board books the 2050 entry into service with no engine dependency, so +0.89 assumes an engine is fitted.
- A one-year wait to 2051 would lower the value, and that case is not on this grid.
- Profile §11.2 read the same case the same way: a Rolls-Royce commitment in our launch year makes us wait a year, and that failed. Its numbers are superseded.

tests.name: A320 ramp shield

tests.numbers:

- No ramp problem is reported.

tests.name: Delay Tactics (rules 4 and 5, five pillars)
tests.threshold: At most one move, only after an fps launch and before its entry into service. 'Both' counts as two. Bottleneck only as a first claim on our own capacity. Poaching only while an Airbus programme is in development.
tests.numbers:
This fails for any move. The lean, at none, passes.

- One move with an A350 Re-engine: -11.46 / -0.09 / -0.08 / +0.22 / -0.09 / -11.46 / -0.09.
- A second move adds -0.19 to -0.27.
- It is short of $1B in every column.
- On the hold row nothing is in development, because NGSA is in service, so poaching also breaks rule 5.
- Bottleneck and both breach the integrity pillar.

tests.name: Production readiness, rule 1 and engine maturity slip (NGSA)
tests.threshold: No NGSA entry into service before 2035. On a reported engine slip, re-time NGSA; never cancel it.
tests.numbers:
- NGSA has been in service since 2037, after the 2035 technology year, so rule 1 was met.
- No slip is reported.
- There is nothing to re-time or cancel.

tests.name: Boeing Rate Increase
tests.threshold: No reaction: we keep our own disciplined ramp.
tests.numbers:

tests.name: Next generation: CFM's open-fan line (ask 6; no order on this board)
tests.threshold: Read only, for the Board's strategy off-site. The gates we would apply are a wing buildable at rate, a mature production system, and two engine sources with CFM in the set.
tests.numbers:
- CFM says an open fan comes 'ten years from a launch with an airframer, and not before 2045'. That puts the earliest entry into service at 2055 for a 2045 airframer launch, and 2060 for 2050.
- RISE is not a product, and CFM calls its ducted engine 'not the next generation'.
- The board counts NGSA's market to 2056, 20 years from 2037.
- No second maker has an open-fan line on the record, the Joint Venture included. A successor would not meet our two-source condition today.
- Read: a 2055+ technology question for the off-site, with no programme commitment.

vetoes.plan: A350 Re-engine launched in 2045, entry into service 2050 (option 2)
vetoes.ground:
Failed engine-readiness test (teams.md Step 3 engine test, applied to the public record; inference).

The engine:
- Rolls-Royce, the A350's only maker, has no widebody engine on the record. Launched this round, the UltraFan widebody is ready in 2051 (6 years under rules.md), one year after the 2050 entry into service.
- The only mature widebody upgrade is GE's GEnx (ready 2033). It has never been fitted to an aircraft family that flies Rolls-Royce only.

Grid margin against the best passing option (hold):
- +0.89 in S1-S5, -0.51 / -0.50 in S6-S7, +0.75 weighted.
- That is under $1B in every column, so no override can carry it, and the Board's override review would fail it as well.

Scope:

- It is not a safety, quality, ramp-shield or supply-crunch result.
- The board books the 2050 entry into service with no engine dependency, so this constraint is off-grid.

vetoes.plan: Any Delay Tactics (bottleneck, poaching or both), on the hold row or the Re-engine row
vetoes.ground:
Company red line, rule 4:
- No fps is on the record, so any move is naked and draws the $48.32B fine.

Rule 5: poaching with nothing in development on the hold row.

Integrity pillar: bottleneck and both.

Grid:

- A second move adds -0.19 to -0.27.

Not overridable.

ops.would_change_mind_if:
A350 Re-engine:
- I would pass the engine test only if a Rolls-Royce widebody engine for the A350 were on the public record and ready by the Re-engine's entry into service. For a 2045 launch it would have had to be launched by 2044, and none was.
- If Rolls-Royce launches the UltraFan widebody this round (ready 2051), a 2050 launch (entry into service 2055) would pass my engine test. That window is off-grid and not a promise, and rule 3 closes it if Boeing launches a 787 Re-engine.
- A non-default engine passes only if the grid shows at least $1B over hold.
- A reported supply crunch would fail it on concurrency as well.

Ramp:
- A reported quality escape on NGSA or the extra lines, or a supply event on CFM or Joint Venture engines, work packages, titanium or rare earths, would hold the next rate step and the next extra-line step until the KPIs recover. With 191-249 aircraft of slack, that costs no delivery on the brief's numbers.

A320 tail:
- If engines for any 2046 unit cannot be confirmed without drawing on fleet spares, the tail stops at what is covered.

Delay Tactics:
- Nothing on this board changes bottleneck or both.
- Poaching would come up only once, and only if all of these hold: an fps reaches the record, an Airbus programme is in development, the expected scenario shows at least $1B, and the CEO records that he sets aside the stricter condition.
ops.memo:
My tests are role-derived; none of my record is in my own words (Very low confidence).

I recommend the default: ngsa hold, no engine code (in service), rea350 hold, delay_tactics none, a320_plan alt.

Safety and quality: the brief reports no event on NGSA, the A320 tail or the A350. Pass.

The ramp: capacity 1,328 in 2045, 1,429 in 2047 and 1,489 in 2050, against deliveries of 1,137, 1,180 and 1,250: 191-249 aircraft of slack, no waiting backlog. Each rate step and extra line goes ahead only on its KPIs; a step held back costs no delivery. I hold none back today.

A320 tail: 26 aircraft in 2045, about 52 engines, inside tail supply held to about 2045. Anything later needs an extension that draws no fleet spares. The 2038-2041 pacing measure can close: the line has been demand-bound since 2044.

Engines: the Joint Venture engine in service since 2037, CFM's ducted engine ready since 2041. Certify the ducted standard in sequence, never dropping CFM. No crunch reported.

A350 Re-engine: capacity passes (0 years of overlap, $0 strain), as does A350F absorption. It fails on the engine. Rolls-Royce, our A350 maker, has no widebody engine on the record; launched this round, it is ready in 2051, a year after a 2050 entry into service. The only ready upgrade, the GEnx, is GE's, on a family that flies Rolls-Royce only. A non-default engine needs at least $1B; the grid shows +0.89. Soft veto, binding.

Delay Tactics: red line, binding.

other_moves.move: Talent and recruitment programme (renewed)
other_moves.detail: Staffing for the NGSA ramp to about rate 100 and for each extra-line step comes from new hiring and internal development, trained before the step [A-0366, A-0485]. The programme covers our own hiring only and takes nothing from any rival's workforce.

other_moves.move: Supply security for our own lines (renewed)
other_moves.detail: Keep securing our own work packages, titanium and rare earths for the NGSA ramp and the extra lines [AX-0060, AX-0062, AX-0063]. A320 tail: 2045 is covered by the LEAP-1A and GTF tail supply held to about 2045. Engines for any unit built in 2046 must be confirmed before build without drawing on fleet spares; if they cannot be, the tail stops at what is covered. This is a first claim on our own needs only. The public line names no engine supplier and refers to no past reset.

other_moves.move: Zero-for-zero trade advocacy (renewed)
other_moves.detail: Keep working through industry coalitions for a tariff-free regime on civil aircraft and parts [AX-0088, AX-0046].

other_moves.move: Quality gates on the ramp; close-out of the 2038-2041 pacing measure (Wagner's recommendation, adopted)
other_moves.detail: Each NGSA rate step to about 100 a month, and each extra-line step (5 a month more each year, up to 20), goes ahead only when three gates are met: conformance and concessions at the current rate are flat or improving with zero safety-related escapes; engines from CFM and the Joint Venture and the work packages are on time for the next rate, with no draw on fleet spares; and staffing comes from recruitment. With 191-249 aircraft of slack in 2045-2050 on the brief's numbers, a step held back costs no delivery. The 2038-2041 pacing measure is closed at the Board's twice-yearly safety review on 'no safety, quality or supply event recorded', claiming no KPI figure. No rate or line figure is published. The public line is 'rate by rate, quality first'.

other_moves.move: Engine standards on NGSA: certification in sequence
other_moves.detail: Wagner reports to the Board on the maturity of the Joint Venture engine (in service since 2037) and of CFM's ducted engine (ready since 2041). The ducted standard is certified on NGSA in sequence and cut in only at a rate step whose KPIs are met. The current CFM standard is kept until then, and CFM is never dropped. Two sources (CFM and the Joint Venture) and three makers are kept in 2045 and 2050.

other_moves.move: A350 kept at Do Nothing; widebody watch
other_moves.detail: The A350 Re-engine is held. The record shows a forgone +0.89 in S1-S5, +0.75 on my weights, against -0.51 / -0.50 avoided in S6-S7. The ExCo will look at a 2050 window (entry into service 2055) only if Rolls-Royce puts a widebody engine for the A350 on the public record and no 787 Re-engine is on it. That window is off-grid, held to the same $1B test, and not a promise. On the CFO's inference it is worth about +0.6 at most, so in practice holding closes the path.

other_moves.move: Capital allocation proposal to the Board (CFO)
other_moves.detail: These matters are reserved to the Board. Payout of 48% (the 2025 level), inside the 30-50% policy, recalibrated at each Yearly Budget on audited net cash. Renew the standard AGM buyback authority (18 months, 10%) for share-plan cover only. Any discretionary programme goes to the Board only on audited net cash, not on the stress case. No equity raise and no state money in the case [AX-0022, AX-0102, AX-0001].

other_moves.move: Next-generation technology question at the Board's strategy off-site
other_moves.detail: Wagner reads CFM's open-fan line ('ten years from a launch with an airframer, and not before 2045') as an entry into service of 2055 at the earliest, with no second maker on an open-fan line today. That fails our two-source condition for now. The question goes to the off-site as a roadmap and technology-gate review, with no programme commitment [AX-0006, AX-0020, AX-0073].

decision.public_statement: Our core principles of safety, quality, integrity, compliance and security will remain at the heart of all we do. Our new single-aisle aircraft has been in service since 2037 and is now in a disciplined and controlled ramp-up: rate by rate, quality first, with each step taken only when our quality and supply-chain indicators are met. The last aircraft of the A320 family will leave our lines over the coming period, supported to the end with the same care our customers have known for decades. In widebodies, the A350 family, including the A350F, remains our offer. We continue to assess its evolution as engine technology matures, and we will decide on our own timetable and within our financial discipline. Our programmes are funded from our own cash flow, which preserves our financial flexibility. We are preparing the next generation of aircraft through our technology roadmap with our partners, on technology readiness, not on a calendar. We will keep working with our industry partners for a tariff-free, zero-for-zero regime in civil aerospace.
decision.rationale:
DECISION: the company default.
- ngsa: hold
- ngsa_engine_code: none (NGSA is in service)
- rea350: hold
- delay_tactics: none
- a320_plan: alt
None of these is a Board item. The package and the public statement go to the Board for reading.

WHY, BY MY FOUR QUESTIONS
(1) The five pillars: nothing is covert, and the statement gives windows, not dates, and names no supplier and no internal target [AX-0073, AX-0081, AX-0004, AX-0005].
(2) The ramp: 2045 is the first year of about rate 100, the first extra lines and the last A320s, the delivery priority whose weight rose [AX-0073]. A widebody development adds load in that year for less than $1B.
(3) The 2030s: NGSA has been delivered. I prepare the next generation through the roadmap and the off-site, not through a launch [AX-0020, AX-0006].
(4) The Board: hold carries no item, and the Board approves it.

TEAM RULE, STEP BY STEP
Step 1. Delete red-line and pillar breaches.
- Every Delay Tactics row is deleted. No fps is on the record, so every move is naked (rule 4) and draws the $48.32B fine, about $11.2B in PV.
- One move is -11.45 in S1 and -11.46 in S6 against the same plan without it, and at most +0.22 (S4).
- A second move adds -0.19 to -0.27.
- On the hold row nothing is in development, so poaching also breaks rule 5. Bottleneck and both breach integrity.
- The Board vetoes all three. I do not set aside the team's stricter condition.
- This also deletes the raw S4 best (Re-engine + one move, +11.94).

Step 2. Survivors of both tests.

frame.question:
What game are we playing, and how do we win? [CX-0467]

This round the game is the installed base we already have. There is no new slot to win.
- NGSA has been in service since 2037. Code 7 held, and all three makers are fitted.
- Our Ducted has been ready since 2041, Embraer has counted since 2042, and the GEnx upgrade has counted since 2042. All three can only hold.
- The fps has not launched.
- No order on offer this round wins a slot on this board.

The only live question is whether to launch the Open Fan, alone or with Lobby, ahead of any airframe that could take it.
- A launch now is ready in 2055. That is eighteen years after NGSA entered service, and one year before the board closes the narrowbody window in 2056.
- On the grid it costs $19.22B alone, or $16.92B with Lobby, against hold, in both columns. It earns no share.

So we win by running what we have, in this order:
- Safety and durability of the LEAP, Ducted and GEnx fleets come first as the 737 MAX phases out from 2044.
- Fleet kits and spares get first call on supply.
- RISE stays whole as technology with Safran.
- The balance sheet and the payout stay untouched.
- We give the Board a candid account of 2035 and of the objectives.

"We get paid in dollars, not in percentages" [CX-0630]. I'll tell you what we know and tell you what we don't [CX-0436].

vetoes.ground: Capex, binding grounds 1 and 2. -16.92 / -16.92 against hold ($9B plus $7.92B). It fails pays-for-itself in every column. Its premium of $16.92B exceeds the $15B RISE allowance.
