Even at $17B it would rest on an airframer path that fails in every column, and it buys no objective. Lobby's +2.30 / +2.29 falls with the Open Fan. Note: my veto right is an inference (teams.md §1). It binds unless Culp answers the failed test with evidence.

vetoes.plan: lobby_emissions: launch (alone)
vetoes.ground: Capex, binding ground 1. It is off the grid: $1B with no board effect and no Open Fan launched or live, so -1.00 in each column, below hold. Any emissions or SAF advocacy goes as an unpriced other move. Note: my veto right is an inference (teams.md §1). It binds unless Culp answers the failed test with evidence.

vetoes.plan: Any public statement or other move that offers launch-era pricing or a concession to win an fps code (code 7 against a code-4 fps included), or talks CFM narrowbody price or capacity without Safran. None appears in Culp's draft; I re-test the final text.
vetoes.ground: Terms, binding ground 3 (hard rules 4 and 7). Launch-era pricing is behind us, and narrowbody pricing 'is a joint decision' with Safran. A code-4 fps is worth at most about $1.34B to us on this board, which buys no concession. Note: my veto right is an inference (teams.md §1). It binds unless Culp answers the failed test with evidence.

vetoes.plan: expected_pv_b booked above -25.0, or any public or Board wording that the Open Fan costs '35 points' of NB share
vetoes.ground: Advice, not a veto. Book -25.0: hold less the weighted un-gridded set (about $0.38B), plus a margin, with -26.82 named as the downside. On the objective wording, the 35 points apply on NGSA and floor at our 27.0%. The total-share effect is about 18.6 points in 2045 and 20.2 in 2050 (13.2 and 14.3 with Lobby). Report it that way to the Board.

cfo.would_change_mind_if: Nothing on this grid moves the orders. Hold is best in both columns by $16.92B or more, and no order on offer lifts share. To flip me on the Open Fan, the record would have to show an airframer committed to launching a new narrowbody on it, with entry no earlier than the engine's ready year and inside the 2056 window, and a grid row inside the $15B allowance. That cannot happen this round: a 2045 launch is ready in 2055, and NGSA has been in service since 2037. The booking moves on confirmed data only. I lower it if Boeing launches a 7-year fps on code 4 (up to -$1.34B) or a rival widebody move goes on the record (-$0.41-1.07B). I raise it toward -24.41 once Boeing has stayed out of a window-relevant launch and no widebody move has come by 2050. A safety or durability flag from Ali changes fleet priorities, not these orders. Any launch-era pricing, concession, or price or capacity talk without Safran in the final text is a terms veto.
cfo.memo:
Larry, the short answer: hold every field. Your numbers check.

Open Fan is -19.22 / -19.21 against hold: the $8B bill plus $11.22B of wait. I rebuild that wait at $11.23B; it is every engine we have on NGSA from 2045 to 2056. No new strain: the $2B is booked. With Lobby it's -16.92 in both columns. Neither pays for itself, and neither fits the $15B allowance, which is declared in full and can't borrow the $2.0B round cap. At $0.8-0.9B a year the payout floor isn't the binding test. Premium $0.0B; game $0.0B of $4.0B.

You asked me to push. One correction: the 35 points floor at our 27% of NGSA, so the Open Fan costs about 19 points of total share in 2045 and 20 in 2050.

On 2035, there's nothing to hide. The Joint Venture is essentially the whole gap. It took our NGSA share at hold from 18.3% to about 13.3% from 2037, roughly $2.96B on both rows. The pair's own gain held, $7.69B against $7.54B promised, so it earned about +1.69 against a Joint-Venture-hit hold near -26.1. Volumes, dates and bills landed as planned. I sized that risk and left it out of the centre. We've been proven wrong on that one before. But the good news is the -27.0 landed $2.59B under the outcome.

Weights 0.70 / 0.30. Un-gridded: a code-4 fps up to $1.34B, widebody moves up to $1.07B, about $0.4B weighted. Book -25.0; downside -26.8. Standard terms, price with Safran.

tests.name: Turn on, turn off: ready year of every engine on the board (Culp ask 3)
tests.threshold: No ready year earlier than the board's development time: Ducted launch + 6; Open Fan launch + 10 and not before 2045; Embraer counts 7 years after launch; GEnx 3 years after launch, not before 2035. An order whose value depends on an earlier year fails. This is my binding date ground (inference).
tests.numbers: Ducted: launched 2035, ready 2041 (2035 + 6). Partner Embraer: launched 2035, counting from 2042 (2035 + 7), riding an engine ready a year earlier. GEnx upgrade: launched 2030, ready 2033 (2030 + 3), counting from 2042. Those three can only hold. Open Fan: a 2045 launch is ready in max(2045 + 10, 2045) = 2055. A 2050 launch would be ready in 2060, past the 2056 NB window. The grid's Open Fan rows (-43.63 / -43.63; with Lobby -41.33 / -41.34) are computed at 2055 and nothing earlier. Hold, the row I recommend (-24.41 / -24.42), adds no ready year. No order on offer depends on a year earlier than launch plus development years, or on an Open Fan before 2045.

tests.name: Test, not analysis: dates in Culp's frame and draft public line (Culp ask 6)
tests.threshold: Every date in the public statement or other moves must be one a test can back: no Open Fan entry before 2045, and no ready date before launch plus development years (binding ground 2, inference).
tests.numbers: The draft public line has no year in it. Its only timing is 'an open fan comes ten years from a launch with an airframer ... No year.' That is launch + 10, the board's floor, so it passes. Dropping 'not before 2045' is right. That year has now arrived, and kept in, it could read as 'available now', which no test backs. Advice, not a veto: say 'no sooner than ten years from a launch with an airframer', as the Board recommended in 2035. 'Comes ten years from' reads closer to a promise, and the RISE fly demo has slipped before (mid-decade, then 'this decade'). The frame's other years (fps EIS 2052 / 2055, window close 2056, Ducted 2041, Embraer and GEnx 2042) are board mechanics for internal use, not public commitments. The draft carries no Ducted year and no time-on-wing figure. At step 4 I veto, on binding ground 2, any statement or move that gives an Open Fan ready or entry year earlier than 2055 for a launch now (for example 'by 2050' or 'early 2050s'), or any ready year earlier than launch plus development years.

tests.name: Ducted gate record: points (b) and (c) (Culp ask 1; the Board's first ask)
tests.threshold: (b) passed on core or engine test before 2041 is used in any statement, customer commitment or the Embraer schedule. (c) accepted by the airframer and the regulator before entry into service. Proof is turn on, turn off on test, never analysis.
tests.numbers: This is a gap in the record, not a pass and not a failure. Neither the brief nor my own record carries a core or engine test result, a regulator or airframer acceptance, or any field data on the Ducted. I cannot report (b) or (c) as passed, and I will not dress analysis up as test. Nothing on the record shows either one failed. What I can confirm from the record: our 2030 and 2035 public statements used no year but 2045. Our 2035 public other moves said 'No ready date' for the Ducted and 'No Embraer volume, price or date'. The only use of 2041 is inside the private gate move, as its own condition. The bulletin's 'ready 2041' and 'ready 2042' are the board's record, not our commitment. The brief has no findings from the private airframer talks, so I cannot confirm whether 2041 was used in a customer commitment. The board has counted the Ducted on NGSA from 2041. That is the game's mechanic, not evidence of acceptance.

tests.name: Durability first: the fleet in service (Culp ask 2)
tests.threshold: No plan trades durability or time on wing for fuel burn or for a date. The bar for the Ducted is harsh time on wing no worse than the mature LEAP-1A, with the CFM56 as yardstick (inference; Culp's line applied to my seat).
tests.numbers: Hold trades nothing. The draft line makes no durability claim: 'keeping engines on wing' is a priority, not a number. Fleet status from my record, with nothing after October 2025: (1) Ducted: no harsh time-on-wing data, so it cannot be compared with the mature LEAP-1A. (2) Yardstick: in 2023, LEAP fleet leaders in harsh service ran about 4,800 cycles, against 7,000-8,000 for the CFM56 in the same environment; in milder service, 9,882 against about 17,000. (3) LEAP-1A: the HPT kit was certified by FAA and EASA in December 2024. It goes into all deliveries and shop visits and improves time on wing more than twofold, to the CFM56 level. (4) LEAP-1B: I said 2025. By July 2025 the kit was in certification for 1H 2026, a year late. The outcome is not in my evidence. (5) GEnx: no in-service durability data in the brief or my record. The upgrade has counted since 2042: WB share 44.8%, 152 engines a year. Kits reach the fleet at shop visits, 'years, not months'.

tests.name: Safety call: cross-functional, any flag to the full Board (Culp ask 2)
tests.threshold: If a problem or an order touches safety or durability, a cross-functional team makes the call, not one person.
tests.numbers: No safety flag and no durability flag. No failure on the record has been turned on and left on. The frame routes any flag to the full Board as a cross-functional call, answered on evidence and never decided by a date. That meets the standard. My condition: a gap in the record is not a pass. Keep the named Ducted hot-and-harsh and dust gate standing as the in-service fleet review. Its members are engineering, quality and supply chain; fleet support with field data; the safety review; and Safran engineering. It should report harsh time on wing for the Ducted, LEAP-1A, LEAP-1B and GEnx to the full Board at each review. Under 'find problems before problems find us', keep enhanced inspection of safety-critical parts in new-make and MRO as the MAX tails off.

tests.name: Ready no later than the airframe: Open Fan (advice; Culp ask 3)
tests.threshold: Report the gap in years. If the Open Fan is ready after the first new NB's EIS, the board takes 35 pp of NB share (20 pp with Lobby). Not a veto ground (inference).
tests.numbers: NGSA, in service since 2037, is the first new NB in both columns. A 2045 Open Fan is ready in 2055, 18 years behind it in S1 and S2. In S2 the fps 10-year enters in 2055, the same year, but NGSA came first, so the wait applies anyway. Against a 7-year fps (EIS 2052, which no column shows) it would be 3 years late. It cannot be ready by the first new NB's entry in any column. A 2050 launch is ready in 2060, past the 2056 window. Against hold: Open Fan -19.22 / -19.21; Open Fan + Lobby -16.92 / -16.92.

tests.name: Ready no later than the airframe: Ducted (advice)
tests.threshold: Report the gap in years. A defensive Ducted ready after the airframe's entry still earns +10 pp from its ready year once a new NB is in service. Not a veto ground (inference).
tests.numbers: The Ducted was ready in 2041, 4 years after NGSA's 2037 entry, and has earned +10 pp on NGSA where CFM is fitted since then. Against any fps it is ready 11 years ahead of a 2052 EIS and 14 years ahead of a 2055 EIS, so it stays on offer to both airframers. Hold only.

tests.name: Physics, and RISE on test (Culp ask 4)
tests.threshold: Call RISE the next generation only at 20% or better. A ducted engine gets 'less than half' the gain, so the Ducted is never the next generation. With no fuel-burn data in the brief, this is a wording check (inference).
tests.numbers: Wording: the draft calls the Ducted 'not the next generation', and RISE keeps the 20% bar. Pass. On RISE, the brief carries no ground or flight-test results. My record stops at: more than 350 programme tests with an early focus on durability (July 2025); dust testing on the compact-core HPT blades, begun October 2025, the earliest GE has started it; open-fan noise below today's LEAP, shown with Airbus (2024); ground and flight test targeted for 'this decade', after the fly demo slipped from 'by the middle of this decade'. The 20% is a design target on physics ('more than 20%'; 'practically impossible ... without the open fan'). It is not a test result. Nothing on test in my record yet backs 20% without trading durability. No product date follows.

tests.name: Supply load: hold, as the 737 MAX phases out (Culp ask 5; doctrine, not my record)
tests.threshold: Two or more projects cost $2B of strain and load the same constrained suppliers. Recommend against stacking unless the grid pays more than the strain (inference; the board's strain rule).
tests.numbers: The $2B strain is already booked (GEnx, Ducted and Embraer are live), and hold adds no project. In 2044 the MAX's LEAP-1B was 569 x 2 = 1,138 engines, 65.5% of our 1,737 NB engines. The other 599 went on Airbus airframes (27.0% of its 2,216). Airbus holds LEAP-1A tail supply for its A320 lines to about 2045. Our NB engines at hold go from 1,737 (2044) to 1,635 (2045, -5.9%), 1,530 (2050, -11.9%) and 1,070 (2055, -38.4%). OE load falls, but the installed LEAP-1B and LEAP-1A fleets still need kits and shop visits. My order: safety first; then fleet kits and spares for LEAP-1A, LEAP-1B, Ducted and GEnx, with spares never crowding out OE. Watch item (inference): as LEAP-1B OE runs down to none by 2060, supplier volume on 1B parts falls while shop-visit demand continues. Contract that spares supply now. My only supplier record is Culp's 2024 description (80% of shortages from 9 suppliers at 15 sites). I have no current data and flag no named supplier. Capacity stays joint with Safran. No evidence in my own words: following doctrine.

tests.name: Supply load: Open Fan, alone or with Lobby (advice)
tests.threshold: A further project must pay on the grid for the load it puts on the constrained suppliers (inference; doctrine).
tests.numbers: On the grid it adds no new strain, but nothing pays for it. Against hold: -19.22 / -19.21 alone ($8B bill plus $11.22B of wait penalty); -16.92 / -16.92 with Lobby ($9B bill plus $7.92B). Physically it would put development parts on the same constrained suppliers while the LEAP-1B fleet's kits and spares need them. Recommend against.

tests.name: Fix, don't redesign
tests.threshold: On the WB, prefer the upgrade on a proven architecture to a new engine. On the NB, keep RISE technology flowing into LEAP while RISE matures. This does not argue against the Open Fan as the next generation (inference).
tests.numbers: WB: the GEnx upgrade is live on the GE90/GEnx architecture and holds, with no flag. NB: keep targeted component upgrades flowing into the LEAP-1A, LEAP-1B and Ducted fleets at shop visits, carrying RISE technology as it matures on test.

vetoes.plan: Conditional, and not in the frame's draft: any public statement or other move that gives an Open Fan ready or entry year earlier than 2055 for a launch now (for example 'by 2050' or 'early 2050s' to meet the objective), or any ready year earlier than launch plus development years.
vetoes.ground: Dates not backed by real testing, binding ground 2. A 2045 launch is ready no sooner than 2055 (2045 + 10), and a 2050 launch no sooner than 2060. The record carries no RISE ground or flight-test result, and the fly demo has slipped before. My veto right over programme dates is an inference: my words are from 2024, as VP of Engineering, on durability-fix results. The team rule makes it binding unless Culp answers it with evidence. The frame's draft ('ten years from a launch with an airframer ... No year') passes, so nothing stands today.

vetoes.plan: open_fan: launch, alone or with lobby_emissions: launch
vetoes.ground: Advice only. The ready year, 2055, passes my date test, so this is not binding. But it is 18 years behind NGSA (in service since 2037) in both columns and level with the S2 fps. Against hold it is -19.22 / -19.21 alone and -16.92 / -16.92 with Lobby. No RISE test result in the record backs a product commitment. It would load the constrained suppliers while LEAP-1B kits and spares need them. Keep RISE all in as funded technology with Safran: no launch ahead of an airframer, no cancel.

vetoes.plan: lobby_emissions: launch alone
vetoes.ground: Advice only. No evidence: following Culp and doctrine. Without an Open Fan it does nothing on the board. For any unpriced advocacy, the technical facts I can supply: RISE is designed to be SAF-ready and hydrogen-capable, and open-fan noise was shown below today's LEAP with Airbus.

vetoes.plan: Public statement wording on the Ducted and the Open Fan
vetoes.ground: Advice only. Durability first is not a date ground. With no test or field data on the Ducted, make no time-on-wing figure and no 'matches LEAP-1A' or 'CFM56-level' claim for it. Never call it the next generation. On the Open Fan, prefer 'no sooner than ten years from a launch with an airframer' to 'comes ten years from', and give no entry year.

ops.would_change_mind_if: Test and field data only, never analysis. (1) Ducted, against: harsh time-on-wing field data below the mature LEAP-1A, or a failure turned on in test or service that the design does not turn off (HPT distress, nozzle coking, dust). I would raise a cross-functional durability flag to the full Board at once. It changes fleet priority and kits, not this round's orders. (2) Ducted, for: core or engine test and regulator and airframer acceptance on the record. I would report gate points (b) and (c) closed and back a durability statement no wider than the test. (3) RISE: ground and flight-test results that turn durability and dust on and off at 20% or better. I would back 'no sooner than ten years from a launch with an airframer' as a commitment. An Open Fan order still needs an airframer, which is Culp's call. (4) Supply: supplier data showing LEAP-1B or LEAP-1A spares and kits slipping at the constrained suppliers as OE runs down. I would raise a supply flag ahead of anything else. Nothing on this grid changes my orders.
ops.memo:
Test, not analysis.

Dates. Every year passes turn on, turn off. Ducted ready 2041, launch plus six. Embraer counting from 2042, plus seven. GEnx ready 2033, counting from 2042. An Open Fan launched now is ready in 2055: eighteen years behind NGSA, level with an S2 fps. A 2050 launch means 2060, past the 2056 window. The date passes. Against the airframe it fails in every column.

The gate, plainly. The brief and my record carry no core or engine test and no field data on the Ducted. I cannot tell you points (b) and (c) passed. Nothing shows they failed. No public statement of ours used 2041 or 2042. Harsh time on wing against the mature LEAP-1A: no data. The yardstick: LEAP ran about 4,800 harsh cycles against 7,000 to 8,000 for the CFM56; the 1A kit more than doubled it. The 1B kit came a year late.

No safety flag. No durability flag: nothing turned on and left on. But a gap in the record is not a pass. Keep the gate standing as the cross-functional fleet review, reporting to the full Board.

RISE. Over 350 tests, dust on the compact core, noise below LEAP. My record ends in 2025. Nothing on test backs 20% yet. That is physics and a target. No product date.

Supply, on doctrine. Hold adds nothing. The LEAP-1B was two-thirds of our 2044 narrowbody engines. As its OE runs down, protect its spares.

Hold every field. No binding veto.

other_moves.move: Fleet first: kits and spares keep first call as the fleets change over
other_moves.detail: Targeted durability upgrades continue into the LEAP-1A and LEAP-1B fleets at shop visits, into the GEnx fleet, and into the new ducted fleet as field data warrants [CX-0607, CX-0422]. Supply order: safety first, then fleet kits and spares, and spares never crowd out new engines [CX-0529]. Lean before capital at the constrained suppliers [CX-0540, CX-0653]. CFM narrowbody capacity decisions are made jointly with Safran [CX-0184]. No time-on-wing figure is published beyond what testing and field data show. Not priced on the board.

other_moves.move: LEAP-1B and LEAP-1A spares tail contracted now, jointly with Safran
other_moves.detail: As LEAP-1B new-engine volume runs down to none by 2060, supplier volume on 1B parts falls while shop-visit demand goes on. In 2044 the 1B was 1,138 of our 1,737 NB engines. Contract the spares and kit supply for the installed LEAP-1B and LEAP-1A fleets now, ahead of any development parts. This is Ali's watch item, and doctrine drives it rather than my record. No supplier is named and there is no current supplier data. Lean before capital. Capacity stays joint with Safran [CX-0613, CX-0633, CX-0184].

other_moves.move: Ducted hot-and-harsh and dust gate kept standing as the in-service fleet review
other_moves.detail: The cross-functional team stays named: engineering, quality and supply chain; fleet support with field data; the safety review; Safran engineering [CX-0012]. At each review it reports to the full Board harsh time on wing for the Ducted, LEAP-1A, LEAP-1B and GEnx fleets, against the mature LEAP-1A with the CFM56 as yardstick. It also reports the status of gate points (b) core/engine test and (c) airframer and regulator acceptance, which the record does not yet evidence. Enhanced inspection of safety-critical parts continues in new make and MRO ('find problems before problems find us'). Any safety or durability flag goes to the full Board at once as a cross-functional call, answered on evidence. A date never decides it [CX-0009, CX-0208].

other_moves.move: RISE all in as a funded technology programme with Safran
other_moves.detail: Ground and flight testing continue jointly, with durability and dust first. RISE is not cancelled for cost, and there is no product launch ahead of an airframer. It becomes a product when an airframer wants it [CX-0469, CX-0205, CX-0174, CX-0398]. The only public timing: an open fan comes no sooner than ten years from a launch with an airframer. No year. The next-generation bar stays at least 20% better fuel burn without trading durability [CX-0217, CX-0208]. Test results go to the Board as they come off test.

other_moves.move: CFM engines offered to both airframers
other_moves.detail: CFM's new ducted engine stays on offer, with LEAP, to both airframers: on the new single-aisle airplane in service and on any new single-aisle airplane Boeing launches. The work with Embraer goes on, non-exclusive, in addition to our two big customers and not in place of either. No airframer is refused or locked out [CX-0587, CX-0185, CX-0564]. No price, volume, capacity or date is published.

other_moves.move: Terms and private airframer engagement for any new single-aisle campaign
other_moves.detail: Standard terms only: no launch-era pricing and no concession to win or hold any engine code, including against a single-source selection [CX-0930, CX-0609]. NB price and capacity are joint decisions with Safran [CX-0184]. Embraer volume, price and capacity stay joint and private until agreed. Platform talks stay private [CX-0586]. Their purpose is first-hand data on Boeing's dual-source requirement and engine code for any new single-aisle, on product and durability, never on price. Findings go to the Board as they come. None are claimed today.

other_moves.move: SAF and emissions advocacy within GE's ordinary public-policy activity
other_moves.detail: Unpriced, with no board order (lobby_emissions held). Support for SAF readiness and sensible emissions policy through industry bodies [CX-0451, CX-0508]. Technical claims stay limited to what test shows: RISE is designed SAF-ready, and open-fan noise has been shown below today's LEAP [CX-0001, CX-0013]. No product date and no rival named.

decision.public_statement:
Safety, quality, delivery and cost, always in that order. That hasn't changed, and it won't.

Let me tell you what we know and what we don't. What we know: the new single-aisle airplane is flying, and CFM is on it with our partner Safran. Our new ducted engine is in service on the airplanes that chose it. It's the right engine for those airplanes, and we offer it to both airframers. It isn't the next generation. That's the open fan. Our work with Embraer goes on too. It adds to what we do for our two big customers and takes nothing away from them.

So job one this year is the fleet. As airlines change over from today's airplanes to the new ones, LEAP, ducted and GEnx engines have to stay on wing. The kits and spares they need get first call, and spares never crowd out the new engines our customers are waiting on. We'll tell you how the fleet is doing when the field data shows it, and not before.

RISE stays a technology program, and we're all in on it with Safran. On the testing we have today, an open fan comes no sooner than ten years from a launch with an airframer. It launches with an airframer, not ahead of one. When that is, it's really not for us to say.

What we don't know is when the next new airplane comes, or what it will ask of us. We don't have a birthright on that order. When it comes, we'll compete for it on the product and on durability.

We're not going for share for its own sake. We get paid in dollars, not in percentages. The balance sheet stays strong, and we keep returning cash to our shareholders.

It's that simple, ain't that hard.
decision.rationale:
WHAT GAME, HOW WE WIN [CX-0467, CX-0319]. This round the game is the installed base we already have. There's no open slot on this board.
- NGSA has flown since 2037 on code 7, with all three makers fitted.
- Our Ducted has been ready since 2041. Embraer and the GEnx upgrade have counted since 2042. All three can only hold.
- The fps hasn't launched.
- The only live lever is a RISE product launch, alone or with Lobby, and on this board it buys nothing.
We win by running what we have:
- safety and durability of the fleet first;
- kits and spares get first call;
- RISE stays whole as technology with Safran;
- the balance sheet and the payout stay untouched;
- the Board gets a straight account.
"We get paid in dollars, not in percentages" [CX-0630].

DECISION: hold on every field (ducted, open_fan, partner_embraer, lobby_emissions, genx).
- This makes no Board item.
- Premium $0.0B. Game total $0.0B of $4.0B. The RISE allowance is unused.
- No overrides.

THE TESTS
(1) Additive and paid for the risk [CX-0301]. Grid, S1 / S2:
- Hold: -24.41 / -24.42. The best plan in both columns.
- Open Fan: -43.63 / -43.63, which is -19.22 / -19.21 against hold. That is its $8B bill plus $11.22B of wait penalty. Ghai rebuilt the wait at $11.23B: every CFM engine on NGSA, 2045 to 2056. It adds no new strain, because the $2B is already booked.
- Open Fan + Lobby: -41.33 / -41.34, which is -16.92 / -16.92 against hold: the $9B bill plus $7.92B.
- Lobby next to the Open Fan alone: +2.30 / +2.29. It falls with the Open Fan.
- Lobby alone: off the grid, -1.00 a column.
- S1 cost of any Open Fan: its whole bill plus the wait, and nothing bought. The worst column is S1, by $0.01B.
- Weighted at 0.70 / 0.30: hold -24.413. The Open Fan is 19.217 behind hold, and Open Fan + Lobby 16.92 behind.

(2) Low case first [CX-0248, CX-0536]. The expected column is S1, from the public record.
- Boeing says the business case "isn't there yet" and gives no date, for the third round running.
- I take Rahul's 0.70 / 0.30 over my own 0.75 / 0.25, as I did in 2035.
- The columns differ by $0.01B, so the call doesn't turn on the weights.

(3) The airframer sets the date (H2) [CX-0205, CX-0469].
- NGSA entered service in 2037. A 2045 launch is ready in 2055 on Ali's test, 18 years behind it, so the wait applies in every column.
- The RISE allowance doesn't fit:
  - $19.22B and $16.92B are both above $15B.
  - The allowance is declared in full and can't borrow the $2.0B round cap.
  - It needs an airframer path, and that fails in every column.
- A 2050 launch would be ready in 2060, past the 2056 window.
- Held.

(4) Ducted only as a defence (H3). Hold only. It is live, offered to both airframers, and never called the next generation.

(5) Can the suppliers carry it [CX-0613, CX-0633]. Hold adds no project, and the $2B strain is already booked. The supply read below comes from doctrine, not my record.

- Lean before capital [CX-0540, CX-0653]. Capacity stays joint with Safran.

(6) Next generation and durability [CX-0217, CX-0208].
- Nothing on test in our record backs 20% yet (Ali). RISE keeps the bar, and there is no product date.
- Hold trades no durability for anything.

(7) Tie-break [CX-0658]. Not needed: hold leads by $16.92B.

SAFETY AND THE DUCTED GATE, CANDIDLY.
- Ali raises no safety flag and no durability flag.
- But the record carries no core or engine test result, no regulator or airframer acceptance, and no Ducted field data. I can't tell the Board that gate points (b) and (c) passed. Nothing shows they failed either. A gap isn't a pass.

  - The board counting the Ducted from 2041 is the game's mechanic, not evidence of acceptance.
  - Whether 2041 went into a private customer commitment, the brief doesn't show, and I won't guess.

It reports harsh time on wing for all four fleets to the full Board at each review, and enhanced inspection of safety-critical parts continues. Any flag goes to the full Board at once. A flag changes fleet priorities and kits, not these orders.
- Yardsticks from the record:
  - In 2023, LEAP ran about 4,800 harsh cycles against 7,000-8,000 for the CFM56.
  - The LEAP-1A kit was certified in December 2024 and more than doubles time on wing.
  - The LEAP-1B kit came a year late. Its outcome is not in the record.

2035 POST-MORTEM. We approved Ducted + Embraer on an S1 row of -21.58 and booked -27.0. Hold today is -24.41.
- R&D ($4B) and strain ($2B) came in as billed. The Ducted (2041) and Embraer (2042) were on time. Volumes landed on Rahul's 2035 estimates.
- So the whole $2.83B is engine value.
- Rahul's read, which I accept: the Joint Venture, formed that same round, took about $2.96B off both rows level. It cut our NGSA share at hold from 18.3% to about 13.3% from 2037. That is the 1.0 pp in 2040, before the Ducted was ready.
- The pair's own gain held: $7.69B against $7.54B promised. In 2044 we hold 27.0% of NGSA, 13.7 points over a Joint Venture-world hold, against the 13.4 estimated.
- Against the hold we'd actually have had (about -26.08), the pair earned about +1.7.
- Nothing else is in the gap.
- So the decision held up and the forecast didn't. We named the Joint Venture as a $1.8-4.2B risk and left it out of the centre.
- The -27.0 booking landed $2.59B low, but for the wrong reasons: it provisioned for S2 and a slip that never came. This time the provision is sized to named moves.

BOOKING: -25.0, following Ghai.
- Start from hold at -24.41.
- Take about $0.38B weighted for named un-gridded moves:
  - a code-4 fps: about $0.02B weighted, up to $1.34B;
  - widebody rival moves: about $0.36B weighted. A Trent 1000 upgrade is -$0.41B to -$0.75B; UltraFan WB is -$0.50B to -$1.07B; the end of the GEnx fit gain is about $0.35B.
- Add a $0.21B margin.
- Named downside: -26.82, a 7-year code-4 fps plus UltraFan WB.
- I raise the booking only on confirmed data.

SAFRAN GATE (CFM parity):
- Hold needs no gate.
- RISE continuing as joint funded technology is joint practice.
- The Ducted offered on any fps on standard terms is joint practice: meeting an airframer's launch with an engine. Price and capacity stay joint [CX-0184].
- Open Fan and Lobby are not brought. A RISE product launched ahead of any airframer, waiting in every column, is outside joint practice, and I see no reason Safran would agree.
- GEnx is GE alone.

BIASES, NAMED:
- The installed-base lens [CX-0555] likes a RISE launch as "seeding the next 30 years". I book none of that, because the board's NB window closes in 2056.
- Deference to airframers [CX-0452] could make us late on a code-4 fps. On this board the answer is the Ducted on offer, standard terms, and private talks on product and durability.
- Money guided low: the booking is -25.0.
- Ramp optimism isn't triggered: no ramp is promised.
- Doctrine, not my record, drove the supply read, the LEAP-1B spares contract, and how Lobby and advocacy are handled.

EXCO:
- Rahul's tests all pass on hold. His binding vetoes fall only on plans I'm not bringing.
- I re-tested the final text against his terms veto. It has no price, no concession, and no price or capacity talk.
- Ali's date tests pass. His conditional date veto doesn't bite: the statement carries no year.

WHAT CHANGES IT IN 2050: nothing on this grid.
- An Open Fan launched in 2050 is ready in 2060, past the window.
- A safety or durability flag changes fleet priorities, not orders.
- A Boeing code-4 launch or a widebody rival move lowers the booking. We have no order on this board to answer either. The answer is the product, the fleet and the offer.

final.public_statement:
Safety, quality, delivery and cost, always in that order. That hasn't changed, and it won't.

Let me tell you what we know and what we don't. What we know: the new single-aisle airplane is flying, and CFM is on it with our partner Safran. Our new ducted engine is in service on the airplanes that chose it. It's the right engine for those airplanes, and we offer it to both airframers. It isn't the next generation. That's the open fan. Our work with Embraer goes on too. It adds to what we do for our two big customers and takes nothing away from them.

So job one this year is the fleet. As airlines change over from today's airplanes to the new ones, LEAP, ducted and GEnx engines have to stay on wing. The kits and spares they need get first call, and spares never crowd out the new engines our customers are waiting on. We'll tell you how the fleet is doing when the field data shows it, and not before.

RISE stays a technology program, and we're all in on it with Safran. On the testing we have today, an open fan comes no sooner than ten years from a launch with an airframer. It launches with an airframer, not ahead of one. When that is, it's really not for us to say.

What we don't know is when the next new airplane comes, or what it will ask of us. We don't have a birthright on that order. When it comes, we'll compete for it on the product and on durability.

We're not going for share for its own sake. We get paid in dollars, not in percentages. The balance sheet stays strong, and we keep returning cash to our shareholders.

It's that simple, ain't that hard.
final.rationale:
WHAT GAME, HOW WE WIN [CX-0467, CX-0319]. This round the game is the installed base we already have. There's no open slot on this board.
- NGSA has flown since 2037 on code 7, with all three makers fitted.
- Our Ducted has been ready since 2041. Embraer and the GEnx upgrade have counted since 2042. All three can only hold.
- The fps hasn't launched.
- The only live lever is a RISE product launch, alone or with Lobby, and on this board it buys nothing.
We win by running what we have:
- safety and durability of the fleet first;
- kits and spares get first call;
- RISE stays whole as technology with Safran;
- the balance sheet and the payout stay untouched;
- the Board gets a straight account.
"We get paid in dollars, not in percentages" [CX-0630].

DECISION: hold on every field (ducted, open_fan, partner_embraer, lobby_emissions, genx).
- This makes no Board item.
- Premium $0.0B. Game total $0.0B of $4.0B. The RISE allowance is unused.
- No overrides.

THE TESTS
(1) Additive and paid for the risk [CX-0301]. Grid, S1 / S2:
- Hold: -24.41 / -24.42. The best plan in both columns.
- Open Fan: -43.63 / -43.63, which is -19.22 / -19.21 against hold. That is its $8B bill plus $11.22B of wait penalty. Ghai rebuilt the wait at $11.23B: every CFM engine on NGSA, 2045 to 2056. It adds no new strain, because the $2B is already booked.
- Open Fan + Lobby: -41.33 / -41.34, which is -16.92 / -16.92 against hold: the $9B bill plus $7.92B.
- Lobby next to the Open Fan alone: +2.30 / +2.29. It falls with the Open Fan.
- Lobby alone: off the grid, -1.00 a column.
- S1 cost of any Open Fan: its whole bill plus the wait, and nothing bought. The worst column is S1, by $0.01B.
- Weighted at 0.70 / 0.30: hold -24.413. The Open Fan is 19.217 behind hold, and Open Fan + Lobby 16.92 behind.

(2) Low case first [CX-0248, CX-0536]. The expected column is S1, from the public record.
- Boeing says the business case "isn't there yet" and gives no date, for the third round running.
- I take Rahul's 0.70 / 0.30 over my own 0.75 / 0.25, as I did in 2035.
- The columns differ by $0.01B, so the call doesn't turn on the weights.

(3) The airframer sets the date (H2) [CX-0205, CX-0469].
- NGSA entered service in 2037. A 2045 launch is ready in 2055 on Ali's test, 18 years behind it, so the wait applies in every column.
- The RISE allowance doesn't fit:
  - $19.22B and $16.92B are both above $15B.
  - The allowance is declared in full and can't borrow the $2.0B round cap.
  - It needs an airframer path, and that fails in every column.
- A 2050 launch would be ready in 2060, past the 2056 window.
- Held.

(4) Ducted only as a defence (H3). Hold only. It is live, offered to both airframers, and never called the next generation.

(5) Can the suppliers carry it [CX-0613, CX-0633]. Hold adds no project, and the $2B strain is already booked. The supply read below comes from doctrine, not my record.
- Our NB engines go from 1,737 (2044) to 1,635 (2045), 1,530 (2050) and 1,070 (2055).
- The LEAP-1B was 1,138 of the 1,737 in 2044. New-engine volume falls; the fleets in service don't.
- Order: safety first, then kits and spares for LEAP-1A, LEAP-1B, Ducted and GEnx. Spares never crowd out OE [CX-0529].
- Contract the LEAP-1B spares tail now (Ali's watch item).
- Lean before capital [CX-0540, CX-0653]. Capacity stays joint with Safran.

(6) Next generation and durability [CX-0217, CX-0208].
- Nothing on test in our record backs 20% yet (Ali). RISE keeps the bar, and there is no product date.
- Hold trades no durability for anything.

(7) Tie-break [CX-0658]. Not needed: hold leads by $16.92B.

SAFETY AND THE DUCTED GATE, CANDIDLY.
- Ali raises no safety flag and no durability flag.
- But the record carries no core or engine test result, no regulator or airframer acceptance, and no Ducted field data. I can't tell the Board that gate points (b) and (c) passed. Nothing shows they failed either. A gap isn't a pass.
- What I can confirm:
  - No public statement of ours used 2041 or 2042.
  - The 2035 public moves gave no Ducted ready date and no Embraer date.
  - The board counting the Ducted from 2041 is the game's mechanic, not evidence of acceptance.
  - Whether 2041 went into a private customer commitment, the brief doesn't show, and I won't guess.
- My answer on evidence: the gate stays standing as the cross-functional in-service fleet review [CX-0012]. It reports harsh time on wing for all four fleets to the full Board at each review, and enhanced inspection of safety-critical parts continues. Any flag goes to the full Board at once. A flag changes fleet priorities and kits, not these orders.
- Yardsticks from the record:
  - In 2023, LEAP ran about 4,800 harsh cycles against 7,000-8,000 for the CFM56.
  - The LEAP-1A kit was certified in December 2024 and more than doubles time on wing.
  - The LEAP-1B kit came a year late. Its outcome is not in the record.

2035 POST-MORTEM. We approved Ducted + Embraer on an S1 row of -21.58 and booked -27.0. Hold today is -24.41.
- R&D ($4B) and strain ($2B) came in as billed. The Ducted (2041) and Embraer (2042) were on time. Volumes landed on Rahul's 2035 estimates.
- So the whole $2.83B is engine value.
- Rahul's read, which I accept: the Joint Venture, formed that same round, took about $2.96B off both rows level. It cut our NGSA share at hold from 18.3% to about 13.3% from 2037. That is the 1.0 pp in 2040, before the Ducted was ready.
- The pair's own gain held: $7.69B against $7.54B promised. In 2044 we hold 27.0% of NGSA, 13.7 points over a Joint Venture-world hold, against the 13.4 estimated.
- Against the hold we'd actually have had (about -26.08), the pair earned about +1.7.
- Nothing else is in the gap.
- So the decision held up and the forecast didn't. We named the Joint Venture as a $1.8-4.2B risk and left it out of the centre.
- The -27.0 booking landed $2.59B low, but for the wrong reasons: it provisioned for S2 and a slip that never came. This time the provision is sized to named moves.

BOOKING: -25.0, following Ghai.
- Start from hold at -24.41.
- Take about $0.38B weighted for named un-gridded moves:
  - a code-4 fps: about $0.02B weighted, up to $1.34B;
  - widebody rival moves: about $0.36B weighted. A Trent 1000 upgrade is -$0.41B to -$0.75B; UltraFan WB is -$0.50B to -$1.07B; the end of the GEnx fit gain is about $0.35B.
- Add a $0.21B margin.
- Named downside: -26.82, a 7-year code-4 fps plus UltraFan WB.
- I raise the booking only on confirmed data.

SAFRAN GATE (CFM parity):
- Hold needs no gate.
- RISE continuing as joint funded technology is joint practice.
- The Ducted offered on any fps on standard terms is joint practice: meeting an airframer's launch with an engine. Price and capacity stay joint [CX-0184].
- Open Fan and Lobby are not brought. A RISE product launched ahead of any airframer, waiting in every column, is outside joint practice, and I see no reason Safran would agree.
- GEnx is GE alone.

BIASES, NAMED:
- The installed-base lens [CX-0555] likes a RISE launch as "seeding the next 30 years". I book none of that, because the board's NB window closes in 2056.
- Deference to airframers [CX-0452] could make us late on a code-4 fps. On this board the answer is the Ducted on offer, standard terms, and private talks on product and durability.
- Money guided low: the booking is -25.0.
- Ramp optimism isn't triggered: no ramp is promised.
- Doctrine, not my record, drove the supply read, the LEAP-1B spares contract, and how Lobby and advocacy are handled.

EXCO:
- Rahul's tests all pass on hold. His binding vetoes fall only on plans I'm not bringing.
- I re-tested the final text against his terms veto. It has no price, no concession, and no price or capacity talk.
- Ali's date tests pass. His conditional date veto doesn't bite: the statement carries no year.

WHAT CHANGES IT IN 2050: nothing on this grid.
- An Open Fan launched in 2050 is ready in 2060, past the window.
- A safety or durability flag changes fleet priorities, not orders.
- A Boeing code-4 launch or a widebody rival move lowers the booking. We have no order on this board to answer either. The answer is the product, the fleet and the offer.

frame.question:
Control what you can control. In 2045 there is nothing to buy and nothing to cancel on the board. `gtf2_solo` and `jv_with_rr` both offer only `hold`:
- GTF2 folded into the Joint Venture in 2035;
- the Joint Venture formed that same year, so withdrawal is no longer legal;
- the Joint Venture engine has been ready since 2036 and is fitted on NGSA, in service since 2037.
No order of ours goes to the Board this round.

The bad news first. Credibility is met, but Capitalise is not, and no order on the grid can meet it.
- We book -2.16 against the status quo.
- That is $0.63B below the -1.53 we booked in 2035, and $2.84B below the +0.68 shown in the round-2 S4 column, which we rightly did not book.
- The damage sits in the transition years: 2039-40 ran $1.2B and $1.0B nominal below the status quo.
I own that number, and I want the ExCo record to say where it came from.

So the question for 2045 is not what to order but what to run well and how to report it:
1. The in-service record of the Joint Venture engine on NGSA, and of the GTF tail on the A320neo: durability, life-limited parts, time on wing, AOG.
2. Parts and capacity for a ramp from 830 P&W narrowbody engines in 2045 to 925 in 2049 (1,010 by 2052), gated on fleet spares.
3. The formed Joint Venture's terms and governance.
4. An fps campaign on standard terms, if Boeing launches.
5. The freed capital, in the order dividend, debt, buybacks.
6. A public statement brought up to the public record, with an honest account of the $2.16B.

My starting answer: hold/hold, with no spend, no premium and no concession to chase the Capitalise gap. I want Mitchill and Eddy to test that answer, and to bring the in-service and cash record the Board will read in 2050.

frame.initial_lean:
LEAN
`gtf2_solo: hold`, `jv_with_rr: hold`, `premium_b` 0, `overrides` empty. This is subject to Eddy's proposal and technical check and to Mitchill's four-ground gate. It is not a Board item.
- Expected about -2.164 on my provisional weights (S1 0.60, S2 0.40); booked -2.16; expected column S1.

WHY
- It is the only legal row, and it meets my safety constraint: the Joint Venture engine is ready and in service on NGSA [PX-0035].
- Visible demand is not in play, because there is no launch to make [PX-0109].
- Miss a cycle [PX-0071]: if Boeing launches on code 7, we are already in it and the engine is ready. The board values that at -0.01. That rule is RTX-wide and applying it here is inference; any value past 2056 is recorded, not booked.
- Responsible bet [PX-0010]: no premium, because nothing trails.
- Value, not share: standard terms; no discount to win the fps or to chase Capitalise.
- Objectives: credibility met; Capitalise not met, at -2.16. I say so plainly and spend nothing to chase it.

BIASES, DECLARED
- Incrementalism: I lean to Boeing holding. The MAX phase-out is the counter, so I hold S2 at 0.40, not lower. The weights barely move the answer.
- Operating optimism: GTF2's 2036 date held. I still publish no time-on-wing figure and no block-upgrade date.
- Architecture loyalty: GTF2 is the engine in service. The gear and core stay ours.

OTHER MOVES I PROPOSE
- B1 (public): Hot Section kit continues at shop visits, charged on standard terms.
- B2 (public): standard terms for any fps campaign, and the Joint Venture engine offered only where ready by EIS.
- B3 (private): ramp gated on fleet spares.
- B4 (private): formed Joint Venture terms to the Finance Committee, and an annual Joint Venture NPV review.
- B5 (private): in-service durability report to Governance and Public Policy, and the T1 block-upgrade rule.
- B6 (private): capital order.

BOARD
I expect to take up all eight of its 2045 recommendations. At the decision I will also answer each of the seven round-2 review recommendations in `board_response`:
1. 'Equal shares' wording: dropped from the statement.
2. Durability report at certification and before NGSA's EIS: those dates fell between Board rounds. Eddy's report goes to Governance and Public Policy now, in arrears.
3. 2045 standing-commitment review: closed. The Joint Venture formed, withdrawal is illegal, and R&D is $2.00B with no second share.
4. Joint Venture terms to Finance: formation came in the same round as our commitment, so the terms go now, in arrears, and I say so.
5. NGSA seat: held. We are fitted.
6. Capital after 2035: covered by Mitchill's envelope check.
7. Capitalise: stated plainly.

PROPOSED DISCLOSURE (my voice; for Mitchill's ground 4 and Eddy's durability check)
"The bad news first. The move from one generation of single-aisle aircraft to the next cost us volume. Our share of narrowbody engines dipped in 2039 and 2040 before it came back to about a quarter. We own that. The GTF fleet still flying on the A320neo comes first: time on wing, parts, and our customers' aircraft back in the air. The GTF Advantage hot section keeps going into that fleet at shop visits, and new production never crowds out its spares. Control what you can control.

The Joint Venture with Rolls-Royce formed in 2035, when both partners had committed. Its engine has been ready since 2036, built on GTF2, and it is in service on NGSA. Our gear and the GTF Advantage core are Pratt & Whitney modules, designed and built by Pratt & Whitney, and they stay ours. Rolls-Royce speaks for itself. Any change to the engine in service comes only after its own durability campaign is complete. If the testing needs more time, the testing gets it. We have learned our lesson from the prior iterations of the GTF.

We offer the Joint Venture engine to an airframer only where it is ready by that airframe's entry into service, and it is ready now. We compete on standard terms, on the product and on the durability record. We're not in the early entry phase, the launch phase. The airframers speak for their own programmes, dates and engine choices, and we will not get out ahead of them. These are responsible bets with responsible paybacks."

The statement claims no Capitalise result, return figure, time-on-wing figure, block-upgrade date or Rolls-Royce terms, and names no NGSA rate or fps detail. If Mitchill reads the last line as a payback claim, it goes.

tests.numbers:
The miss
- Booked -1.53 in 2035; now -2.16. That is a $0.63B miss, all in engine value (+0.47 to -0.16); R&D was -2.00 both times.
- Against the unbooked S4 forecast of +0.68, the gap is -2.84.
- Bridge: -1.53 + 2.21 (Joint Venture forms: S4 - S1 on the 2035 grid) - 2.84 (what S4 left out) = -2.16.

This brief against the 2035 table (PV at 2026; rounded table -0.57, brief -0.63)
- 2037-40: +0.14 (2037 +0.1, 2039 +0.1, 2040 +0.3 nominal).
- 2041-44: -0.16.
- 2045-56: -0.56 (forecast).
- From 2042, 30 to 51 fewer P&W engines a year.

Drivers
(a) A320-to-NGSA step-down: 0 in the drift; it sits in the level. The 2035 table already had 2039-40 at -1.3 and -1.3 nominal against the status quo (-0.72 PV). Actual was -1.2 and -1.0 (-0.61 PV). Foreseen, and booked in the -1.53.
(b) CFM's ducted engine (ready 2041) and Embraer partnership (2042): the only priced difference between S4 and the outcome, so the whole -2.84.
- On the rules' share arithmetic (NGSA share 38.3% -> 33.3% -> 31.7%; inference), about three-quarters is the ducted engine (about $2.2B) and one-quarter Embraer (about $0.7B).
- The ducted engine was foreseeable. CFM's 2030 public move offered 'a new engine committed alongside a committed airframe', and NGSA was committed in 2030. No column priced it, and my 2035 memo did not name it.
- Embraer was on the rules' menu but had no public signal.
(c) Equal-share rule: +2.21, foreseen and priced in S4.
- On the rules it moves share only on NGSA and the fps; the A320neo keeps CFM 60 / P&W 40.
- On the public record, P&W led RR by 3.8 pp in 2043 (23.4% against 19.6%, about 141 engines: our A320neo tail). The gap closed in 2044 as the tail ran off.
- No sign it took volume the A320neo would have earned us (inference).
(d) Supply and demand: about 0. Total NB engines are within 0.4% of the 2035 table: 3,023 vs 3,023 (2039), 3,631 vs 3,620 (2042), 3,294 vs 3,287 (2045), 3,447 vs 3,456 (2052).

CEO's buckets against the status quo, confirmed
- 2037-38: +0.10.
- 2039-40: -0.61.
- 2041-56: +0.41.
- Net -0.10 on the rounded table against the brief's -0.16, inside the +/-0.33 rounding band.

cfo.would_change_mind_if:
Recorded, not booked; this is my answer to ask 8, looking to 2050.

1. A 2050 brief that offers an order. A launch (a block upgrade or a new programme) would face Committed airframe, Bounded downside and my gate, after Eddy's durability campaign. A cancel or withdraw would face Premature exit. I expect none: the Joint Venture engine is ready and fitted.
2. A Boeing launch on the record. That raises S2 but does not change the order. A code-3 (CFM only) fps, against Boeing's dual-source line, is the one real exposure, and I would price it in 2050. A 7-yr fps (EIS 2052) brings more fps volume inside 2056.
3. A CFM Open Fan launch. Under the public rules, NGSA entered service before any Open Fan is ready, so CFM would lose 35 pp of NB share (20 pp with lobbying) to the others. That is upside for us, not booked until it is on the record.
4. The 2045-56 forecast recovery (+0.27 PV) not showing in the years realised by 2050. I reset the booked number in that round, with drivers.
5. Eddy showing that the ramp to 925 needs capital. I test it against Do Nothing and a buyback at 10%.
6. Evidence that the equal-share rule takes volume the A320neo would have earned us, for example P&W at or below RR while the A320neo tail still delivers. I would revise driver (c).
7. Joint Venture terms that drift towards a balancing payment, a carried share or below-standard modules: ground 3.
8. The statement keeping 'responsible paybacks': ground 4 until it is struck.
cfo.memo:
Low end first. One legal row, hold/hold: -2.16 (S1), -2.17 (S2). My weights are S1 0.65, S2 0.35. Boeing's lead indicators have moved: the MAX phases down from 2044 and Boeing's share is 30.4%. But "the business case isn't there yet", and there is no date. Expected -2.1635, booked -2.16. Nothing to fund. 2045 adds $0 of R&D, the fold wrote off $0, and total R&D is $2.00B, our share. There is no second share. Dividend first, then debt back to pre-ASR levels, then buybacks. The stretch was never used.

Now the miss, plainly. My first read, and Chris's, was the transition. It wasn't. The transition was already in the -1.53 we booked in 2035, and 2037-40 came in about $0.14B better than that table. The $0.63B is more pervasive: 30 to 51 fewer engines a year from 2042, when CFM's ducted engine and its Embraer partnership start to count. Market volume is within 0.4% of the 2035 table, so this is share, not demand. On the 2035 grid the Joint Venture was worth +2.21; CFM took back 2.84. CFM told us in 2030 it would meet a committed airframe with a new engine. I priced "rivals hold" anyway. That one's mine.

Of the "recovery", +0.14 is realised and +0.27 is forecast. I won't call it recovered.

Gate: hold/hold clears all four grounds. One line fails ground 4: "responsible paybacks", with -2.16 booked, reads as a payback claim. Strike it. Build capacity for 925, not for the 1,010 peak.

ops.proposal:
ORDERS PROPOSED: gtf2_solo: hold; jv_with_rr: hold. These are the only values the brief offers (round3.md section 3). No Board item, premium_b 0, overrides empty. I confirm the CEO's reading and have nothing to add on the orders.

WHY hold on gtf2_solo. GTF2 launched in 2030 and folded into the Joint Venture when it formed in 2035, writing off $0. No solo programme is left to launch or cancel. The Joint Venture engine inherited GTF2's ready year, 2036, and has been in service on NGSA since 2037. Hold keeps the engine we tested as the engine in service.

WHY hold on jv_with_rr. The Joint Venture formed in 2035, and the rules allow withdrawal only before formation. Hold keeps P&W fitted on NGSA (code 7, fitted CFM + PW + RR) and keeps code 4 open to Boeing. Grid row hold/hold: -2.16 (S1), -2.17 (S2). Weights do not change my technical view.

ANSWERS TO THE CEO'S ASKS

(1) Orders: hold/hold, confirmed. Not submitted: withdraw, cancel, launch, launch_if_selected.

(2) In-service record of the Joint Venture engine (GTF2 as tested) on NGSA since 2037, for Governance and Public Policy. I report against the gates we set in 2030 and 2035 and invent no figures.
- On the public record:
  - GTF2's 2036 date, set at launch in 2030, held to the year; the Joint Venture engine is ready since 2036;
  - it was fitted at NGSA's 2037 EIS and is still fitted;
  - no P&W quality escape, slip or AOG problem is published for 2035-2044.
- Gate (a), an Advantage derivative with gear and core carried over: consistent with the record ("GTF2 is what we bring"; the Joint Venture engine kept GTF2's schedule). A changed configuration would have reset the clock.
- Gates not on the board and not in my evidence: (b) the severe-environment endurance hours (target at least the Advantage's 2-3x the base programme), (c) life-limited parts at full life at EIS, time on wing, shop-visit rate, AOG count and Hot Section kit embodiment. Governance and Public Policy should take the internal certification records (life-limited part lives, endurance hours, instrumentation of every new feature), not my word.
- Last figures in my evidence, all from June 2023: 10% of the fleet AOG [PX-0120], about 350 AOG on average projected through 2026 [PX-0300], 60% of the fleet in the latest configuration [PX-0116].
- The share dip to 22.1% (2039) and 22.8% (2040) comes from board mechanics (the A320 step-down, CFM's ducted engine, the equal-share rule). This board does not make it a durability signal.
- The report falls in arrears. The Board's round-2 ask for reports at certification and before NGSA's EIS fell between Board rounds, and I say so. From now on the report goes every year, not only at Board rounds.
- My bias, declared: I will not say "there's no surprise coming". I said that in June 2023, and the recall came five weeks later [PX-0112][PX-0290]. The powder-metal cause was found only by a records review [PX-0039]. So the report includes a supplier records review before each ramp step (inference).

(3) T1 status.
- The pre-2041 window closed with the engine in service as GTF2 as tested, on the record.
- No Rolls-Royce-content block upgrade is planned or proposed by me. I do not want one now: engineering stays on the in-service fleets.
- On this board, fitment depends only on being ready by EIS and on the code. CFM's ducted engine (+10 pp) is already in the year table, and an upgrade earns nothing on the board.
- Against CFM's ducted engine (ready 2041) on an fps entering service around 2055: whether a block upgrade is needed to compete is a product question for Calio. If it is wanted, it comes the way Block D and the Advantage kit came [PX-0116][PX-0088]:
  - its own completed severe-environment campaign, instrumented, with full-life parts at its own entry into service [PX-0128][P-1214];
  - staffed from the Joint Venture, not fleet engineering;
  - no date before the testing, and the date gives.
- Running hotter for fuel burn trades against time on wing [P-1360]. This is seat doctrine, not my record.

(4) The GTF tail on the A320neo.
- The A320neo flies CFM 60% / P&W 40%. Airbus held GTF tail supply to about 2045.
- On the Alt plan the A320 lines step down over about eight years from NGSA's 2037 EIS, so GTF OE ends about now (inference from rules.md).
- The installed base was over 10,000 engines, including orders and options, in 2023 [PX-0129]. It needs spares and shop visits for decades after OE ends; that is the fleet that comes first.
- The Hot Section kit (about 90-95% of the Advantage durability content [PX-0088]) continues at shop visits, charged on standard terms [PX-0100]. Its embodiment percentage in 2045 is not in evidence, and I give none.

(5) Parts and capacity. P&W NB engines from the brief's year table: 830 (2045), 866, 861, 887, 925 (2049), 913, 987, 1,010 (2052), then 916 (2053) falling to 574 (2060).
- Ramp size:
  - +11.4% to 2049 and +21.7% to 2052, about 2.7-2.8% a year;
  - 925 is 6.6% above our delivered peak of 868 (2043); 1,010 is 16.4% above it;
  - the largest single step is +74 engines (+8.1%) in 2051. The +141 (+20.1%) step of 2041 was absorbed with no escape on the record.
  - From the 2052 peak, volume falls 17% by 2056 and 43% by 2060.
- Pacing parts, from my record: about 30 GTF parts [PX-0123], led by structural castings [PX-0125], and the powder-metal disk material behind the 2015 HMI ramp escape [P-1040]. The full 2045 list is not in my evidence. Because the Joint Venture engine is GTF2 (an Advantage derivative), its OE and the GTF fleet's spares draw on the same constrained material (inference).
- The gate is confirmed: the ramp is gated on GTF and Joint Venture fleet spares, worked at a daily cadence and reported to the ExCo weekly [PX-0131][PX-0099]. The fleet beats new volume [PX-0080].
- Meet it lean, not with capital. Shops wait on parts, not on shop capacity [PX-0124]. Material freed by the end of GTF OE goes first to spares, then to Joint Venture OE (inference). Supply-base steps come in increments, as castings +40% did [PX-0125]. Permanent capacity sized for a 2052 peak would sit 43% idle by 2060.
- No capacity spike: new supplier capacity gets qualification, first-article inspection and a records review before it ships [P-1040]. I have no capital ask in 2045. If the 2051 step needs supplier capacity, it goes to Mitchill in 2050, priced against Do Nothing and against a buyback.

(6) fps readiness. The Joint Venture engine has been ready since 2036.
- A 7-year fps launched in 2045 enters service in 2052: 16 years of margin.
- A 10-year or Embraer fps enters service in 2055 (the S2 column): 19 years of margin. Both pass.
- Technical conditions on a code-4 or code-7 installation:
  - (a) offered in the as-tested configuration; any fps-specific change gets its own durability campaign first;
  - (b) the new installation (nacelle, installation loads, flight test) is real certification work the board does not model; it is staffed from the Joint Venture, not fleet engineering;
  - (c) fps volume sits behind the fleet-spares gate. Code 4 would put more fps engines on P&W than code 7, so the gate binds harder there (inference).
- Nothing on Boeing's dates, code or site.

(7) Engineering load. No development runs on the board and there is no strain charge. Fleet engineering stays on three jobs: Joint Venture fleet support on NGSA, the GTF tail and the Hot Section kit. No block upgrade or fps installation draws on it (T4 carries forward). Pass.

(8) My veto check on the orders, other moves and draft statement:
- Ground 1 passes and Ground 2 passes. No veto.
- B1, B2, B3 and B5: pass on my grounds. I add to B3 and B5 the supplier records review and qualification before each ramp step.
- B4: passes the architecture test; the terms are Mitchill's ground 3. B6 and B7 are not my grounds.
- The statement makes no "full life" or time-on-wing claim, and that is correct. Do not add "every life-limited part at full life" unless the certification records confirm it.
- "Ready since 2036", "in service on NGSA" and "ready now" match the bulletin.
- "Any change ... only after its own durability campaign is complete" is T1 in public words.
- "New production never crowds out its spares" is a rule we control, not an outcome claim. Keep it, and keep to it.
- "Responsible paybacks" is Mitchill's call, not mine.

tests.numbers: No live P&W fleet, quality or supply problem in the 2045 bulletin or brief, and no launch is ordered. ops.would_change_mind_if:
Any of these would change my view:
- A P&W quality escape, slip or rising AOG on the Joint Venture engine or the GTF fleet, in the 2050 bulletin or brief or in the internal records. I would contain first with a dated recovery, hold each ramp step behind fleet spares, and fail ground 2 on anything that drops the gate.
- Certification records showing a life-limited part not at full life at NGSA's EIS, or development testing left open at service. I would report it to Governance and Public Policy at once and strike any public durability claim (ground 1 on the wording).
- Any ask to put a Rolls-Royce-content block upgrade or fps-specific change into service before its own completed campaign, or to compress testing. Ground 1, binding.
- A 2051 step (+74 engines) that cannot be met lean. I would bring supplier capacity to Mitchill against Do Nothing and a buyback, never as a spike.
- A 2050 brief offering a new launch or exit. I would re-run readiness by EIS on it.
Weights do not move my technical view.
ops.memo:
The bad number first. We book -2.16 against the status quo. In 2039-40 our share fell to 22.1% and 22.8% while the A320 stepped down. That's not a durability number, but I own the operating side.

Orders: hold and hold, the only legal values. GTF2 folded in 2035, and the Joint Venture formed that year.

Readiness passes. The Joint Venture engine has been ready since 2036, GTF2's launch-plus-six date, and in service on NGSA since 2037. Against an fps launched now, that's 16 years of margin at a 7-year EIS and 19 at a 10-year. That date held. My Advantage date didn't, so I still discount my own dates.

In service: the board shows no escape, no slip and no AOG count. I publish no time-on-wing figure. I won't say there's no surprise coming; I said that once, five weeks before a recall. Governance gets the certification records and a supplier records review.

Parts: 830 engines this year, 925 in 2049 and 1,010 in 2052, then down 43% by 2060. That's under 3% a year, and 16% over our 2043 peak. Parts pace it, not shops. Meet it lean, gate it on fleet spares, work it daily and report it weekly. No capacity spike: the powder-metal escape came out of a ramp. The fleet comes first.

No block upgrade without its own completed durability campaign. The date gives.

Where I'm thin: one event in 2023, before the recall. After that, it is seat doctrine, not my record.

other_moves.detail: No game-board effect. The fleet comes before new volume [PX-0080][PX-0088][PX-0106]. The kit is charged, not given away [PX-0100]. No embodiment percentage and no time-on-wing figure are published (Eddy: neither is in evidence; Mitchill ground 4). The installed base needs spares and shop visits for decades after GTF OE ends, around 2045. Material freed by the end of GTF OE goes first to spares and then to Joint Venture OE (Eddy, inference).

other_moves.move: Standard commercial terms for any fps campaign; the Joint Venture engine offered only where it is ready by the airframe's entry into service
other_moves.detail: No launch-style discount, concession or free upgrade [PX-0055][PX-0100]. A rival's discount does not move the answer. The Joint Venture engine has been ready since 2036, so it meets any fps entry into service: 2052 on a 7-year programme, 2055 on a 10-year one. It is offered in its as-tested configuration. Any fps-specific change gets its own durability campaign first, and the installation work is staffed from the Joint Venture, not fleet engineering (Eddy T4). fps volume sits behind the fleet-spares gate. The grid prices S2 at -0.01 against S1, so there is nothing to buy. Nothing is said on Boeing's dates, code or site [PX-0062].

other_moves.move: Narrowbody OE ramp gated on GTF and Joint Venture fleet spares, met lean
other_moves.detail:
P&W NB engines rise from 830 (2045) to 925 (2049) and 1,010 (2052), then fall to 838 (2056) and 574 (2060). The ramp is gated on GTF and Joint Venture fleet spares, worked daily and reported to the ExCo weekly [PX-0131][PX-0099]. The fleet beats new volume [PX-0080]; supply-first [PX-0085].
- We hold capacity for about 925 a year, which is sustainable. We bridge the 2051-52 peak (987-1,010) lean, with no permanent capex, because capacity sized for that peak would sit 43% idle by 2060 (Mitchill, Eddy).
- No capital ask in 2045. If the 2051 step (+74 engines) needs supplier capacity, it goes to Mitchill in 2050, priced against Do Nothing and against a buyback at 10%.
- New supplier capacity gets qualification, first-article inspection and a supplier records review before it ships, and before each ramp step [P-1040][PX-0039]. Pacing parts: about 30, led by structural castings and powder-metal disk material [PX-0123][PX-0125].
- Dropping the gate would trigger Eddy's ground-2 veto, which is binding.

other_moves.move: Joint Venture governance after formation: formed terms to the Finance Committee, and an annual Joint Venture programme NPV review with the Board
other_moves.detail:
The 2045 standing-commitment review closes. The Joint Venture formed in 2035, so withdrawal is no longer legal. GTF2's $2.00B counted toward P&W's share, the fold wrote off $0, and there is no second $2B share.

The formed terms go to the Finance Committee as a significant transaction. They go in arrears, because formation came in the same round as our commitment:
- gear and GTF Advantage core stay P&W-owned, P&W-designed, P&W-built modules, with no licence or transfer [P-1233];
- no cash or balancing payment to Rolls-Royce;
- P&W does not carry Rolls-Royce's share;
- P&W's economic share is not below half;
- P&W modules are supplied at standard terms;
- the GTF risk-sharing partners sit behind P&W's half in their existing proportions, and no partner money is booked until it is signed [P-1563][PX-0037][PX-0038].
Any drift from these terms triggers Mitchill's ground-3 veto, which is binding.

The annual Joint Venture NPV review follows Mitchill's format:
1. ΔPV against Do Nothing at the 10% WACC, with the booked S1 figure shown beside any weighted figure.
2. The low end first, naming any unpriced rival move.
3. The variance against last year, by driver.
4. Cash by year.
5. Any new spend, against Do Nothing and a buyback, after Eddy's durability campaign.
6. A recorded-not-booked list.

Equal-share effect recorded: P&W and Rolls-Royce each took 24.1% of NB engines in 2044. P&W led by 3.8 pp in 2043 on the A320neo tail. There is no sign the rule took A320neo volume from us (Mitchill, inference).

other_moves.move: In-service durability report on the Joint Venture engine and the GTF tail to Governance and Public Policy, from now on every year; T1 for any block upgrade
other_moves.detail:
Eddy reports against the 2030 and 2035 gates, from the record only. The Joint Venture engine is GTF2 as tested. Its 2036 date held from launch, it was fitted at NGSA's 2037 EIS and it is still fitted. No P&W quality escape, slip or AOG problem is published for 2035-2044.

The committee takes the internal certification records rather than our word: life-limited part lives, endurance hours, instrumentation of every new feature, time on wing, shop-visit rate and AOG count. A supplier records review comes before each ramp step. The report is in arrears: the round-2 asks at certification and before NGSA's EIS fell between Board rounds.

T1: any Rolls-Royce-content block upgrade, or any fps-specific change, enters service only after its own completed, instrumented severe-environment campaign, with full-life parts. Testing is never compressed, and the date gives [PX-0073][PX-0035][P-1214]. No block upgrade is proposed in 2045. If a quality escape appears, we contain first, give a dated recovery, and the committee hears the bad number first.

Capitalise on the record: the booked number reset with its drivers, and the low-end lesson

Booked -2.16, a $2.16B gap. It is $0.63B below the -1.53 booked in 2035 and $2.84B below the unbooked round-2 S4 forecast of +0.68.

The bridge (Mitchill): -1.53 + 2.21 (the Joint Venture, priced in S4) - 2.84 (CFM's ducted engine, about 2.2, and its Embraer partnership, about 0.7, both launched in 2035 and in no column) = -2.16.
