- The ducted engine was foreseeable from CFM's 2030 public line. The ExCo priced 'rivals hold' anyway, and I own that as the one who framed it.

From now on, any engine a rival has named in a public move is priced as a low end, even when no grid column carries it [PX-0076].

Recovery, worded as proven: of the +0.41 PV for 2041-56, +0.14 is realised (2041-44) and +0.27 is forecast (2045-56). If the forecast does not show in the years realised by 2050, the booked number is reset in 2050, with its drivers. No premium, discount or concession chases the gap.

decision.public_statement:
The bad news first. The move from one generation of single-aisle aircraft to the next cost us volume. Our share of narrowbody engines dipped in 2039 and 2040 before it came back to about a quarter. Our competitors answered with new engines of their own, as they should, and what we have earned on the money we spent to get here has come in short of what we planned. We own that, and we are not going to dress it up.

The GTF fleet still flying on the A320neo comes first: time on wing, parts, and our customers' aircraft back in the air. The GTF Advantage hot section keeps going into that fleet at shop visits, and new production never crowds out its spares. Control what you can control.

The Joint Venture with Rolls-Royce formed in 2035, when both partners had committed. Its engine, built on GTF2, has been ready since 2036 and is in service on NGSA. Our gear and the GTF Advantage core are Pratt & Whitney modules, designed and built by Pratt & Whitney, and they stay ours. Rolls-Royce speaks for itself. Any change to the engine in service comes only after its own durability campaign is complete. If the testing needs more time, the testing gets it. We have learned our lesson from the prior iterations of the GTF.

We offer the Joint Venture engine to an airframer only where it is ready by that airframe's entry into service, and it is ready now. We compete on standard terms, on the product and on the durability record. We're not in the early entry phase, the launch phase. The airframers speak for their own programmes, dates and engine choices, and we will not get out ahead of them. The development spend is behind us. What we control now is how this engine runs in service.
decision.rationale:
DECISION
- Orders: `gtf2_solo: hold`, `jv_with_rr: hold`.
- `premium_b` $0 and `overrides` empty.
- Expected PV -2.1635 on the governing weights, S1 0.65 and S2 0.35. Worst column S2, -2.17. Booked -2.16 (S1).
- Not a Board item. Both fields offer only `hold` (round3.md section 3), the Board never vetoes a hold, and a round of all holds does not reach review.

1. STARTING POINT. Eddy proposes hold/hold. Mitchill recommends the same, and it was my framing lean. It is the only legal row:
- GTF2 folded into the Joint Venture in 2035 and wrote off $0;
- the Joint Venture formed in 2035, so withdrawal is barred;
- launch, launch_if_selected, cancel and withdraw are not offered and are not submitted (Board would-veto list).

2. STRIKE. No binding veto stands against the orders.
- Mitchill's ground-4 veto binds on one line of my draft statement: "These are responsible bets with responsible paybacks." He is right. In 2030 and 2035 the line described bets not yet made. In 2045 the bet is made and booked at -2.16 against Do Nothing, so "payback" claims a return the record does not show. I struck it and used his replacement: "The development spend is behind us. What we control now is how this engine runs in service." This is a revision within his veto, not an override.
- Mitchill's ground-3 veto (Joint Venture terms, fps terms) is conditional and not triggered. The formed terms and the fps campaign stay on standard, risk-and-investment-only lines.
- Eddy invokes no veto. His conditional ground-1 veto (any change before its own durability campaign) and ground-2 veto (dropping the spares gate) are not triggered, and both are written into the private moves.
- Nobody flags a red-line breach.

3. CONSTRAINT FIRST [PX-0035][PX-0073]. Eddy's readiness check binds on me, and it passes.
- The Joint Venture engine has been ready since 2036. It was fitted at NGSA's 2037 EIS, with one year of margin, and it is still fitted.
- An fps launched now would enter service in 2052 (7-year) or 2055 (10-year), giving 16 or 19 years of margin.
- GTF2's 2036 date, set at launch in 2030, held to the year. That is counter-evidence to my record of slipped dates [PX-0017][PX-0087], with the H1 2025 date also met [PX-0078]. I still discount my operating dates, and I publish no time-on-wing figure and no block-upgrade date.
- The in-service record passes on the public record only: no escape, slip or AOG problem is published for 2035-44. The board models none of these, and Eddy invents no figures.
- Eddy asked whether a block upgrade is needed to compete with CFM's ducted engine on a 2055 fps. My answer: not now.
  - No upgrade is proposed. The board pays nothing for one, and the fleet beats a new engine [PX-0080].
  - If Boeing launches and the product needs one, it comes as a durability campaign first, staffed from the Joint Venture, and goes to Mitchill against Do Nothing and a buyback.

4. OPTIMISE. There is one row, so there is nothing to optimise; I record the tests.
- Weights. I adopt Mitchill's 0.65/0.35 as the governing set, because I trust his numbers over my own read [teams.md section 4]. My frame had 0.60/0.40. I had pushed S2 up to offset my own incrementalism, while he counts a Boeing launch only once it is on the record. The difference in expected value is $0.0005B.
- Visible demand [PX-0109]: there is no launch to make.
- Miss a cycle [PX-0071]: we are in this cycle, fitted on NGSA. If Boeing names code 7 (or code 4, now open), we are in that one too, ready.
  - The rule is RTX-wide, and applying it here is inference.
  - Recorded, not booked, as context only: the round-2 grid priced leaving the cycle (cancel GTF2) at -18.09 against -1.53, and losing the NGSA seat (code 5) at $14.69B below S1. That is what staying in protected. It is not a return, and it is not claimed publicly.
- Responsible bet [PX-0010]: no premium, because nothing trails.
- Dividend safe [PX-0081]: Mitchill confirms the dividend is covered, debt is on its path, $0 of the envelope is used and the stretch is unused.
- Value, not share [PX-0055][PX-0100]: standard terms, and no concession to win the fps (S2 is worth -0.01) or to chase Capitalise.

5. CAPITALISE, STATED PLAINLY. It is not met: -2.16 booked, a $2.16B gap that no order on the grid can close.
- The components are engine value -0.16 and R&D -2.00, undiscounted. On the board's valuation, the Joint Venture engine roughly holds our status-quo volume, and the $2.00B of development is not recovered by 2056.
- The drift is $0.63B below the 2035 booked -1.53 and $2.84B below the unbooked S4 forecast of +0.68.
- My frame had the source wrong, and Mitchill corrects it.
  - The A320-to-NGSA transition was already in the -1.53 level. The 2035 table carried 2039-40 at -1.3 and -1.3 nominal; actual was -1.2 and -1.0, slightly better.
  - The miss is share from 2042: 30 to 51 fewer P&W engines a year, as CFM's ducted engine (ready 2041, about $2.2B) and its Embraer partnership (2042, about $0.7B) start to count.
  - The bridge: -1.53 + 2.21 (Joint Venture) - 2.84 (CFM) = -2.16. Volume is within 0.4% of the 2035 table.
- The ducted engine was foreseeable. CFM said in 2030 that it would meet a committed airframe with a new engine. I framed 2035 on "rivals hold" and leaned on the S4 column without naming CFM's answer as the low end. Mitchill owns his memo; I own the frame. "Always paranoid about competition" [PX-0076] should have applied.
- My frame's "recovered about two-thirds" overstated, and I withdraw it. Of the +0.41 PV for 2041-56, +0.14 is realised (2041-44, 23% of the -0.61 transition) and +0.27 is forecast.
- In public, the shortfall is owned without a figure, and the statement claims no Capitalise result.

6. CAPACITY. The ramp from 830 to 925 engines (2049) is met lean and gated on fleet spares. Capacity for about 925 is sustainable. The 2051-52 peak (987-1,010) is bridged lean, because it falls 43% by 2060. There is no capex ask, and supplier qualification and a records review come before each step. The ramp is base-business capacity: the status quo also needs about 925 engines in 2049. It is not a Joint Venture return.

7. BIASES, DECLARED.
- Operating optimism: checked by the 2036 date holding, and still discounted.
- Incrementalism: I lean to Boeing holding, so the governing weights put S2 at 0.35, not lower.
- Architecture loyalty: the gear and core stay ours, and the engine in service stays GTF2 as tested.
- Value capture: no concession.

8. FOR 2050 (recorded, not booked):
- a Boeing launch on the record (a code-3 fps is the one real exposure);
- a CFM Open Fan launch, which is upside under the public rules;
- the +0.27 forecast recovery failing to show, which would mean a reset with drivers;
- the 2051 step needing supplier capacity;
- any drift in the Joint Venture terms;
- any order a 2050 brief offers, which would face the Board's Committed airframe, Bounded downside and Premature exit tests, and Mitchill's gate.

Doctrine, not my record: the Joint Venture governance and terms (no evidence of my own on Rolls-Royce; P-1233 and Mitchill's ground 3), and the readiness and parts views (deferred to Eddy).

- His drift decomposition replaces mine. I had blamed the transition. He shows it sat in the 2035 level, and that the $0.63B miss is share lost from 2042 to CFM's ducted engine and Embraer partnership, which no column priced. Volume is within 0.4%. I accept it, and I own the frame that set 'rivals hold'.
- His ground-4 veto on 'responsible bets with responsible paybacks' is binding and right. The line is struck and his replacement is used.
- His advice, not binding, on 'two-thirds recovered' is taken: realised +0.14, forecast +0.27.

- His seat rests on one event, June 2023, before the recall. Beyond it, his views are seat doctrine, and I weigh them as such, though they match company doctrine (T1, the spares gate, P-1040).

final.public_statement:
The bad news first. The move from one generation of single-aisle aircraft to the next cost us volume. Our share of narrowbody engines dipped in 2039 and 2040 before it came back to about a quarter. Our competitors answered with new engines of their own, as they should, and what we have earned on the money we spent to get here has come in short of what we planned. We own that, and we are not going to dress it up.

The GTF fleet still flying on the A320neo comes first: time on wing, parts, and our customers' aircraft back in the air. The GTF Advantage hot section keeps going into that fleet at shop visits, and new production never crowds out its spares. Control what you can control.

The Joint Venture with Rolls-Royce formed in 2035, when both partners had committed. Its engine, built on GTF2, has been ready since 2036 and is in service on NGSA. Our gear and the GTF Advantage core are Pratt & Whitney modules, designed and built by Pratt & Whitney, and they stay ours. Rolls-Royce speaks for itself. Any change to the engine in service comes only after its own durability campaign is complete. If the testing needs more time, the testing gets it. We have learned our lesson from the prior iterations of the GTF.

We offer the Joint Venture engine to an airframer only where it is ready by that airframe's entry into service, and it is ready now. We compete on standard terms, on the product and on the durability record. We're not in the early entry phase, the launch phase. The airframers speak for their own programmes, dates and engine choices, and we will not get out ahead of them. The development spend is behind us. What we control now is how this engine runs in service.
final.rationale:
DECISION
- Orders: `gtf2_solo: hold`, `jv_with_rr: hold`.
- `premium_b` $0 and `overrides` empty.
- Expected PV -2.1635 on the governing weights, S1 0.65 and S2 0.35. Worst column S2, -2.17. Booked -2.16 (S1).
- Not a Board item. Both fields offer only `hold` (round3.md section 3), the Board never vetoes a hold, and a round of all holds does not reach review.

1. STARTING POINT. Eddy proposes hold/hold. Mitchill recommends the same, and it was my framing lean. It is the only legal row:
- GTF2 folded into the Joint Venture in 2035 and wrote off $0;
- the Joint Venture formed in 2035, so withdrawal is barred;
- launch, launch_if_selected, cancel and withdraw are not offered and are not submitted (Board would-veto list).

2. STRIKE. No binding veto stands against the orders.
- Mitchill's ground-4 veto binds on one line of my draft statement: "These are responsible bets with responsible paybacks." He is right. In 2030 and 2035 the line described bets not yet made. In 2045 the bet is made and booked at -2.16 against Do Nothing, so "payback" claims a return the record does not show. I struck it and used his replacement: "The development spend is behind us. What we control now is how this engine runs in service." This is a revision within his veto, not an override.
- Mitchill's ground-3 veto (Joint Venture terms, fps terms) is conditional and not triggered. The formed terms and the fps campaign stay on standard, risk-and-investment-only lines.
- Eddy invokes no veto. His conditional ground-1 veto (any change before its own durability campaign) and ground-2 veto (dropping the spares gate) are not triggered, and both are written into the private moves.
- Nobody flags a red-line breach.

3. CONSTRAINT FIRST [PX-0035][PX-0073]. Eddy's readiness check binds on me, and it passes.
- The Joint Venture engine has been ready since 2036. It was fitted at NGSA's 2037 EIS, with one year of margin, and it is still fitted.
- An fps launched now would enter service in 2052 (7-year) or 2055 (10-year), giving 16 or 19 years of margin.
- GTF2's 2036 date, set at launch in 2030, held to the year. That is counter-evidence to my record of slipped dates [PX-0017][PX-0087], with the H1 2025 date also met [PX-0078]. I still discount my operating dates, and I publish no time-on-wing figure and no block-upgrade date.
- The in-service record passes on the public record only: no escape, slip or AOG problem is published for 2035-44. The board models none of these, and Eddy invents no figures.
- Eddy asked whether a block upgrade is needed to compete with CFM's ducted engine on a 2055 fps. My answer: not now.
  - No upgrade is proposed. The board pays nothing for one, and the fleet beats a new engine [PX-0080].
  - If Boeing launches and the product needs one, it comes as a durability campaign first, staffed from the Joint Venture, and goes to Mitchill against Do Nothing and a buyback.

4. OPTIMISE. There is one row, so there is nothing to optimise; I record the tests.
- Weights. I adopt Mitchill's 0.65/0.35 as the governing set, because I trust his numbers over my own read [teams.md section 4]. My frame had 0.60/0.40. I had pushed S2 up to offset my own incrementalism, while he counts a Boeing launch only once it is on the record. The difference in expected value is $0.0005B.
- Visible demand [PX-0109]: there is no launch to make.
- Miss a cycle [PX-0071]: we are in this cycle, fitted on NGSA. If Boeing names code 7 (or code 4, now open), we are in that one too, ready.
  - The rule is RTX-wide, and applying it here is inference.
  - Recorded, not booked, as context only: the round-2 grid priced leaving the cycle (cancel GTF2) at -18.09 against -1.53, and losing the NGSA seat (code 5) at $14.69B below S1. That is what staying in protected. It is not a return, and it is not claimed publicly.
- Responsible bet [PX-0010]: no premium, because nothing trails.
- Dividend safe [PX-0081]: Mitchill confirms the dividend is covered, debt is on its path, $0 of the envelope is used and the stretch is unused.
- Value, not share [PX-0055][PX-0100]: standard terms, and no concession to win the fps (S2 is worth -0.01) or to chase Capitalise.

5. CAPITALISE, STATED PLAINLY. It is not met: -2.16 booked, a $2.16B gap that no order on the grid can close.
- The components are engine value -0.16 and R&D -2.00, undiscounted. On the board's valuation, the Joint Venture engine roughly holds our status-quo volume, and the $2.00B of development is not recovered by 2056.
- The drift is $0.63B below the 2035 booked -1.53 and $2.84B below the unbooked S4 forecast of +0.68.
- My frame had the source wrong, and Mitchill corrects it.
  - The A320-to-NGSA transition was already in the -1.53 level. The 2035 table carried 2039-40 at -1.3 and -1.3 nominal; actual was -1.2 and -1.0, slightly better.
  - The miss is share from 2042: 30 to 51 fewer P&W engines a year, as CFM's ducted engine (ready 2041, about $2.2B) and its Embraer partnership (2042, about $0.7B) start to count.
  - The bridge: -1.53 + 2.21 (Joint Venture) - 2.84 (CFM) = -2.16. Volume is within 0.4% of the 2035 table.
- The ducted engine was foreseeable. CFM said in 2030 that it would meet a committed airframe with a new engine. I framed 2035 on "rivals hold" and leaned on the S4 column without naming CFM's answer as the low end. Mitchill owns his memo; I own the frame. "Always paranoid about competition" [PX-0076] should have applied.

6. CAPACITY. The ramp from 830 to 925 engines (2049) is met lean and gated on fleet spares. Capacity for about 925 is sustainable. The ramp is base-business capacity: the status quo also needs about 925 engines in 2049. It is not a Joint Venture return.

7. BIASES, DECLARED.
- Operating optimism: checked by the 2036 date holding, and still discounted.
- Incrementalism: I lean to Boeing holding, so the governing weights put S2 at 0.35, not lower.
- Architecture loyalty: the gear and core stay ours, and the engine in service stays GTF2 as tested.

- the +0.27 forecast recovery failing to show, which would mean a reset with drivers;

Doctrine, not my record: the Joint Venture governance and terms (no evidence of my own on Rolls-Royce; P-1233 and Mitchill's ground 3), and the readiness and parts views (deferred to Eddy).

recommendations.text: In-service maturity and support of the Joint Venture engine. Safety comes first in service as well as before it. Watson should report each round to this Board and to the Safety, Energy Transition & Tech Committee on durability, time on wing, shop-visit rates, spares cover and early-service intervention. He should include the integration of P&W's gear and GTF Advantage core modules, given P&W's own public statement that the GTF fleet still has work ahead. If an in-service issue arises, the fleet comes first and the ramp second. The choice is a fix and a slower ramp, never a shorter inspection or test regime. 'Customer trust and confidence has to be our #1 goal.'

Capacity for the narrowbody ramp without starving the widebody core. The brief shows 830 narrowbody engines in 2045, 866 in 2046 and about 900-1,010 a year to 2052, against 188 widebody engines. Place narrowbody work with high-performing suppliers. Scale partner MRO on the Singapore joint-venture model, together with P&W's shop network. Give widebody time-on-wing work and spares first call on engineering and supply. The readiness and capacity plan goes to the Committee. The off-grid point of 'widebody never starved' is engineering and supply, not money.

The widebody core. Hold both widebody fields this round. Defend widebody share (55.2% from 2042, after the GEnx upgrade) through time on wing inside the existing envelope, on the model of the Trent 1000 durability package. While the Joint Venture is on the record, the $5B strain makes any widebody programme a $5B entry fee for the rest of this game (inference from the brief). A widebody case therefore comes to us in 2050 only if a 787 or A350 Re-engine is on the record and the item value, strain counted, fits the $1B UltraFan WB sub-cap or the $3B cap. Watch S3, where Airbus's widebody airframe share falls to 40.2% by 2050. Report the franchise numbers each round.

The capital frame and the narrowbody bound. McCabe should report narrowbody development money as final at $5.71B: the $4B Joint Venture share plus the $1.71B written off at the 2035 fold. That is $1.71B over the $4B bound, stated openly; no order this round can change it. No further narrowbody development spend is planned, so the gross R&D envelope can return to broadly flat. Narrowbody engine cash goes through the capital order: the balance sheet, then the 30-40% payout, then investment and further distributions on fit, value and timing. No equity, no leverage for distributions. Any change to medium-term guidance comes to this Board before release.

Joint Venture terms and commercial discipline. The Joint Venture formed in 2035, both partners committed in the same round, and the round-2 `withdraw` test is overtaken; please answer it as such. Offer the Joint Venture engine to any airframer only on standard terms, agreed jointly with P&W. An fps selection is worth -0.01 against S1 on this grid, so no launch-style discount, concession or free upgrade can pay. Any change to the Joint Venture terms, or any inducement, comes to this Board with McCabe's co-signature. Profit and cash over market share.

Disclosure. Replace last round's line that UltraFan for the narrowbody is 'in development on its own clock', which no longer fits the record. Say that the Joint Venture engine is in service and that our focus is maturity and time on wing, on the narrowbody fleet and on the Trent fleet. Give no date or engine choice for Boeing's fps or any Re-engine, and nothing on Airbus's ramp. Speak for ourselves only on the Joint Venture, consistent with P&W's stated terms. Announce no widebody programme. 'We won't do anything not profitable' stands.

- UltraFan WB: ready in 2051. It earns only once a re-engined 787 or A350 is in service: never in S1-S2, from 2051 in S3-S4.
- All hold: the Joint Venture engine already earns. Lifecycle value is $12.6B nominal in 2045 against $5.3B under the status quo.

tests.name: Premium against the PV-best order
tests.threshold: Price every premium in $B. Above $3B a round, the PV-best order applies. UltraFan WB sub-cap: $1B.
tests.numbers:
- Hold is best in every column: S1 +9.98, S2 +9.97, S3 +9.98, S4 +10.23. Premium $0.
- Upgrade gap: $6.48B, beyond the $3B cap.
- UltraFan WB gap: $8.88B, beyond both the $1B sub-cap and the $3B cap.
- No declared premium can carry either item.

tests.name: Bounded narrowbody risk (objective, stated openly; not a sign-off ground)
tests.threshold: Our own NB development money, committed or written off, of at most $4B.
tests.numbers:
NOT met. Final at $5.71B: the $4B Joint Venture share plus the $1.71B fold write-off, $1.71B over the bound.
- The same in every row and column; no order this round can change it.
- No further narrowbody development spend is planned.
- It is $2.29B below the $8.0B we carried in round 2.

tests.name: Capital frame for the narrowbody value
tests.threshold: Balance sheet, then the 30-40% payout, then investment and further distributions on fit, value and timing. Nothing is automatic. Guide low, with no straight lines.
tests.numbers:
Lifecycle value, nominal, against the status quo:
- 2045: $12.6B against $5.3B (+7.3).
- 2050: $14.9B (+8.9).
- 2052: $16.6B (+10.4), the peak.
- 2055: $16.1B (+9.5).
- 2060: $14.2B (+6.8).
The CEO's 'about $16B by 2052' is $16.6B. The value peaks with NB engines at 1,010 in 2052, then falls to 574 engines by 2060 as the replacement wave passes, so it does not follow a straight line.

Lifecycle value is engine price x 1.6, so most of it arrives over the engine's life through flying hours. I measure it as net LTSA balance growth, not as in-year cash.

No equity, and no leverage for distributions. Any guidance change goes to the Board before release.

tests.name: Off-grid: an in-service issue on the P&W modules
tests.threshold: Price it as far as the brief allows; otherwise state it as unpriced (inference).
tests.numbers:
Unpriced. The figures below give scale only (inference):
- About $7.5B of the $12.6B 2045 lifecycle value is narrowbody. The widebody part is about 188/197 of the $5.3B status quo, roughly $5.1B.
- Each 10% of a year's narrowbody deliveries deferred moves about $0.75B nominal to the right. A slower ramp defers value rather than losing it.
- Who bears a module fix depends on Joint Venture terms that are not on the record. P&W owns the modules and supplies them at standard terms.
- I book no cost and no upside.
- On this board the widebody base is untouched by a narrowbody issue, so the balance sheet holds.
Fleet first, ramp second.

tests.name: 2050 break-even for a widebody item (forward look, not an order)
tests.threshold: The Re-engine gain needed for a widebody item, with the strain counted, to fit the $1B UltraFan WB sub-cap or the $3B cap (inference).
tests.numbers:
The board books R&D and the strain undiscounted. A 2050 launch therefore costs $9B (UltraFan WB: $4B + $5B) or $7B (upgrade: $2B + $5B) in every column.

Gain needed:
- To fit the caps: about $8B PV for UltraFan WB and about $4B for the upgrade.
- To beat hold: $9B and $7B.

This grid's best gains: UltraFan WB +0.98 (S4) and +0.72 (S3); upgrade +0.52 to +0.54.

A 2050 launch earns for fewer years and is discounted further. The upgrade would count from 2053, and UltraFan WB would be ready in 2056 against a Re-engine EIS no earlier than 2055.

No Re-engine on this board gets there.

tests.name: Round-2 `withdraw` test
tests.threshold: Bring `withdraw` against keeping the commit in 2045 (Board, round 2).
tests.numbers:
Overtaken.
- Both partners committed in 2035 and the Joint Venture formed that round. A withdraw is possible only before formation.
- NB money fell from $8.0B to $5.71B.
- The formation on a fully spent engine in 2045 that we feared did not happen.
- NGSA flies the Joint Venture engine, so it is not an orphan.

vetoes.plan: `t1000_upgrade: launch`
vetoes.ground:
Hurdle and downside.
- The item against hold is -6.48 / -6.48 / -6.48 / -6.46, and -6.48 on every weight set.
- Its worst column is 3.24x its $2B bill.
- It is -1.48 even before the $5B strain, which the grid already includes.
- The gap is beyond the $3B cap.
I withhold my co-signature, so the order stays `hold`.

vetoes.plan: `ultrafan_wb: launch`
vetoes.ground:
Hurdle and downside.
- The item against hold is -9.00 / -9.00 / -8.28 / -8.02, -8.88 weighted, far beyond the $1B UltraFan WB sub-cap.
- Its unselected column (no Re-engine) is -9.00, 2.25x its $4B bill.
- It buys no WB share by 2050.
I withhold my co-signature.

Red-line flag, not a veto ground: no UltraFan launch without a programme that can fly it. No Re-engine is on the record. The CEO should strike it.

vetoes.plan: Any price concession, inducement or change of Joint Venture terms, as an other move
vetoes.ground: Aggressive terms need joint sign-off. An fps selection is worth -0.01 against S1, so no concession can pay. I would withhold my support. As drafted, on standard terms agreed jointly with P&W, this does not apply.

cfo.would_change_mind_if:
Any of these would change my view:
- A 2050 grid shows a widebody item that fits the caps with the $5B strain counted. That needs an A350 Re-engine, or a 787 Re-engine whose maker has publicly named UltraFan, on the record, and a Re-engine gain of at least about $8B PV for UltraFan WB or about $4B for the upgrade. Against this grid's best of +0.98, I do not expect it.
- Watson's in-service report finds a Trent fleet issue that threatens the 50% widebody line. I would fund a fix inside the envelope first; a programme would still have to fit the caps.
- Watson reports an open finding on the Joint Venture engine or on P&W's modules. The orders would not change. I would slow the ramp, rebase narrowbody guidance down, and price the fix before any distribution beyond the 30-40% payout.
- A concession, inducement or change of Joint Venture terms comes forward. I would withhold my support.
- Delivered narrowbody cash (net LTSA growth) runs below the brief's path. I would rebase guidance through the Board.
cfo.memo:
Safety, then the balance sheet. Nothing in these orders touches either.

Narrowbody money is final at $5.71B: our $4B Joint Venture share, met by Solo spend credited at the fold, and $1.71B written off in 2035. That is $1.71B over our $4B bound. Not met, and no order can change it. It is $2.29B below the $8.0B we carried. No further narrowbody development spend; gross R&D goes back to broadly flat.

I recommend hold on every field: +9.98 / +9.97 / +9.98 / +10.23, +9.99 on the weights I confirm (S1 0.75, S2 0.10, S3 0.10, S4 0.05). Hold it at the worst column, +9.97. Premium $0.

I withhold my co-signature on both widebody launches. The upgrade is -6.48 in every column, more than three times its $2B bill, and -1.48 before the strain. UltraFan WB is -9.00 with no Re-engine, -8.88 weighted, against a $4B bill. The Joint Venture is ready and cannot be cancelled, so any widebody programme now pays the $5B strain, about £3.7bn. In 2050 a Re-engine must add about $8B (UltraFan WB) or $4B (upgrade); this grid's best Re-engine gain is +0.98.

The narrowbody value runs through the frame: balance sheet, the 30-40% payout, then investment and distributions on fit, value and timing. It is lifecycle value, not in-year cash, and it peaks around 2052. We guide low. A P&W-module issue is unpriced: fleet first.

My record on engine economics is thin; these are the board's numbers. That's how you should hold it.

tests.name: Ready by EIS: Joint Venture engine (in service)
tests.threshold: The Joint Venture engine is ready at formation + 6, or earlier if a folded Solo is further along. It must be ready by the selecting airframe's EIS. Zero margin passes with a note. A late engine is a fail, but it is advice, not a veto.
tests.numbers: The Joint Venture formed in 2035. The engine was ready in 2036 because it inherited GTF2's schedule (launched 2030 + 6 = 2036). Our folded UltraFan NB (2030 + 7 = 2037) was the slower of the two. NGSA launched in 2030 with EIS 2037, so the margin is 1 year: pass. Under S2, an fps 10-yr launched in 2045 has EIS 2055 on code 5 (RR + CFM), against the engine's 2036 ready date, so 19 years in hand: pass. NOTE FOR THE BOARD: my round-2 condition assumed the folded UltraFan's test schedule would govern. The bulletin shows that GTF2 was further along, so the engine's maturity at entry rested on P&W's full six-year GTF2 programme. P&W's public line was 'durability will be proven before entry into service, with every life-limited part at full life on day one'. That is the rules' ready date earned on a full programme, not compressed maturity, but our assurance on the core and gear now comes through P&W's data. On the round-2 `withdraw` test, Civil's view is that it has been overtaken: the Joint Venture formed in 2035, the engine flies on NGSA, and no withdraw is available.

tests.name: In-service watch: Joint Venture engine and P&W modules (Board ask, inference from the maturity rule)
tests.threshold: No open in-service finding on the record. If one arises, the fleet comes first: a fix and a slower ramp, never a shorter inspection or test regime. I cite no in-service figure I cannot source.
tests.numbers: On the record: EIS on NGSA in 2037, with our first deliveries at 7 (2037), 23 (2038) and 80 (2039), then 257 (2040). Airbus certified 'in sequence, as each one matures', and that slow first ramp gave the early-service intervention window the support plan was built for. RR narrowbody share was 0.2% (2037), 8.4% (2040), 24.1% (2044) and 25.2% (2045). Deliveries ran below last round's projection: 431 against 487 in 2041, 809 against 960 in 2044, and 1,010 against 1,199 at the 2052 peak. That gap matches public moves (CFM's ducted engine from 2041, half its +10 pp from us, and the CFM-Embraer partnership from 2042). Nothing on the record points to an in-service finding (inference). Not on the record: durability, time on wing, shop-visit rates, spares cover and open findings on the Joint Venture engine. The board has no in-service mechanic, so I report none. P&W MODULES: the gear and the GTF Advantage core are P&W-owned, P&W-designed and P&W-built, supplied at standard terms. P&W says 'the GTF fleet still has work ahead of it', with the GTF Advantage hot-section kit going in at shop visits. P&W said that about its own GTF fleet, not about our engine. It is still the closest public evidence on the core we fly. Condition: P&W's module durability data (time on wing, life-limited parts, findings, hot-section kit status) comes through the Joint Venture to the Board and the Safety, Energy Transition & Tech Committee each round. Should anything slow the ramp? Nothing on the record does.

tests.name: Ready by EIS: widebody items (if launched in 2045)
tests.threshold: UltraFan WB is ready at launch + 6 and counts only once a re-engined 787 or A350 is in service. The Trent 1000 upgrade counts at launch + 3 (not before 2035). A late engine is a fail, but it is advice, not a veto.
tests.numbers: UltraFan WB launched in 2045 is ready in 2051. In S3 and S4 a 787 Re-engine launched in 2045 enters service in 2050 (launch + 5), so UltraFan WB is ONE YEAR LATE: a fail, as advice. The board counts it from 2051, not 2050. That is why the 2050 widebody share stays at 55.2% and why its item improves only to -8.28 (S3) and -8.02 (S4), against -9.00 in S1 and S2. In S1 and S2 there is no Re-engine, so it never counts. Trent 1000 upgrade launched in 2045 counts from 2048 (2045 + 3, after the 2035 floor), with no airframe dependency: pass on timing. Forward look to 2050 (inference, from the arithmetic): an UltraFan WB launched in 2050 is ready in 2056, a year after a Re-engine launched the same round (EIS 2055). It can never meet a Re-engine launched in its own round, because 6 years is longer than 5.

tests.name: No early date
tests.threshold: No disclosed EIS or ready date earlier than launch + 7 (UltraFan NB), launch + 6 (UltraFan WB), or the Joint Venture engine's ready date as the bulletin shows it (2036). No time-on-wing target until its risk is gone. Nothing on airframers' dates or P&W's modules beyond P&W's own words.
tests.numbers: The CEO's draft line gives no date. 'Our Joint Venture engine with Pratt & Whitney is in service' matches the record: ready 2036, on NGSA in service since 2037, fitted CFM + PW + RR. It gives no UltraFan WB date, no Re-engine or fps date or engine choice, nothing on P&W's modules and no time-on-wing figure: pass. Dropping 'in development ... no earlier than 2037' is right. It was never early (2030 + 7), but it now describes a folded programme. ADVICE (not a veto ground): keep 'the fleet comes first and the ramp second' as a private rule. In public it can be read as a comment on Airbus's NGSA ramp, or as a hint of an in-service finding that is not on the record. Suggested public wording: 'maturity and time on wing come first, on every fleet we power.'

tests.name: Support before EIS (and in service)
tests.threshold: RR has no narrowbody MRO scale, so a partner-shop support plan had to exist before the narrowbody EIS (by 2036 for a 2037 EIS). In service it must scale with the fleet (inference).
tests.numbers: The plan of record was in place before EIS and the brief reports no slip: services lead since 2030; partner MRO shops on the Singapore joint-venture model by 2032; repair technology, a spare-engine pool and work with high-performing suppliers by 2035; the EIS support team and early-service intervention by 2036. The 2037 EIS therefore had support in place. FLEET SIZE (RR engines delivered): 2,935 by end-2044, 8,217 by end-2050 (2.8 times) and 10,214 by end-2052. For comparison, Trent widebody engines delivered from 2026 to 2050 total 4,844. Is it sized for 2050? I cannot confirm it from the record: the Joint Venture engine's shop-visit rate and time on wing are not published, so the partner MRO and spare pool must be sized on measured rates as the fleet grows 2.8 times. P&W's published Joint Venture terms cover modules, shares and standard terms, not MRO. The shop-visit and spares split for P&W's modules, and the use of P&W's GTF shop network, must be agreed jointly (inference). That is advice, not a veto ground, because support was in place before EIS. For shop visits I use my 1,100-1,200 a year [RX-0279], not 1,400-1,500 [RX-0223]; the two were never reconciled.

tests.name: Engineering load
tests.threshold: A narrowbody project beside a widebody project costs a one-off $5B strain whatever the dates. Red lines: no UltraFan WB beside an UltraFan NB Solo unless both are selected; no Trent 1000 upgrade while an UltraFan is in development (inference, seat and company rule).
tests.numbers: All hold: strain $0 in S1-S4. Confirmed: the Joint Venture is ready and cannot be cancelled, so any upgrade or UltraFan WB now pays $5B for the rest of the game. Upgrade: development 2045-2048. Item value -6.48 / -6.48 / -6.48 / -6.46 (S1-S4), or -1.48 / -1.48 / -1.48 / -1.46 before strain, against a $2B bill; -6.48 on all four weight sets. UltraFan WB: development 2045-2051. Item value -9.00 / -9.00 / -8.28 / -8.02, or -4.00 / -4.00 / -3.28 / -3.02 before strain, against a $4B bill; -8.88 weighted on S1 0.75, S2 0.10, S3 0.10, S4 0.05 (-8.76 with S3 and S4 raised, -8.83 guide-low). The seat red lines do not bite: no UltraFan is in development and no Solo exists. The real overlap: 2045-2052 are the Joint Venture fleet's busiest early-service years (830 rising to 1,010 engines a year). A widebody programme would compete for engineers with in-service support at the worst point (inference). Advice, not binding.

tests.name: Capacity and suppliers
tests.threshold: State RR's engines a year from the brief. The board has no capacity limit, so the result is not applicable. A narrowbody ramp is flagged as needing partner MRO and high-performing supplier capacity (advice).
tests.numbers: Narrowbody engines: 830 (2045), 866 (2046), 861 (2047), 887 (2048), 925 (2049), 913 (2050), 987 (2051) and 1,010 (2052, the peak). They then fall to 916, 903, 869, 838, 751, 674, 623 and 574 (2060), 43% below the peak. Widebody: 188 a year. Total: 1,018 (2045), 1,101 (2050), 1,198 (2052). Narrowbody is 4.4 times widebody in 2045 and 5.4 times in 2052. My midterm widebody OE plan was 300-350 a year [RX-0279], so the 2052 total is 3.4-4.0 times that. Supplier risk: the gear and core come only from P&W, as P&W-owned modules at standard terms, and P&W has said its GTF fleet work comes first. That is concentration on one partner for the two most critical modules (inference). Our own share goes to high-performing suppliers (in 2023, £685m of £2.5bn external spend, 27%) with critical parts dual-sourced, as planned from 2036. Holding the widebody line: Trent kits, spares and time-on-wing engineering are allocated first; narrowbody parts come from the high-performer group; P&W modules come through P&W's own chain. After 2052, OE falls 43% while shop visits rise as the fleet ages, so build the narrowbody aftermarket through partner shops and move OE capacity to repair rather than add owned capacity that idles (inference).

tests.name: Widebody dominance
tests.threshold: RR widebody engine share at least 50% in 2040, 2045 and 2050 (inference). Time on wing is the lever.
tests.numbers: All hold: 58.0% (2040), 55.2% (2045) and 55.2% (2050) in every column S1-S4, 5.2 pp above the line. The GEnx upgrade took 2.8 pp from 2042. With the upgrade: 60.0% in 2050 (+4.8 pp), about $1.35B a point with strain ($0.31B a point before it). With UltraFan WB: 55.2% in 2050 in every column. No column threatens the core. Watch item: in S3, Airbus's widebody airframe share (the A350 fleet we power alone) falls from 41.2% to 40.2% in 2050. Under the rules a lone re-engined 787 gains 1 pp a year from its EIS, so the erosion grows after 2050, although the board does not move our engine share (inference). What time on wing inside the envelope protects: the Trent XWB, about 60% of the large-engine fleet [R-1279]; the Trent 1000 durability package, which could more than double time between scheduled maintenance, with the fleet retrofitted within two years [RG-0068]; and longer-life HP turbine blades and life-limited parts on the Trent 1000 and Trent 7000 [RX-0285]. Together they keep the installed base flying and earning without a programme and without the strain.

tests.name: Technology pull-through
tests.threshold: Qualitative only. UltraFan technology feeds the Trent fleet. No grid adjustment (inference).
tests.numbers: UltraFan NB folded in 2035, but its demonstrator technology (geared architecture, with the Liebherr gearbox joint venture behind it) keeps flowing into Trent time on wing. That is a two-way flow. No value is added to the grid, and it is no reason to launch UltraFan WB.

vetoes.plan: A, the CEO's lean: `ultrafan_nb_solo: hold`, `jv_with_pw: hold`, `ultrafan_wb: hold`, `t1000_upgrade: hold`
vetoes.ground: No Civil veto. (1) Maturity: the Joint Venture engine was ready in 2036 on GTF2's full six-year programme, a year before NGSA's 2037 EIS, so nothing is compressed. No in-service finding is on the record. (2) Early date: the draft line gives no date. (3) Support: the partner-shop plan was in place by 2036, before the 2037 EIS. Advice, not binding: size partner MRO and the spare pool for about 8,200 RR engines by 2050; agree the MRO and spares split for P&W's modules jointly; get P&W module durability data to the Committee each round; keep 'ramp second' out of the public line.

vetoes.plan: B: A + `t1000_upgrade: launch`
vetoes.ground: Not a Civil ground. It counts from 2048 on its full three years, no date is disclosed, and Trent 1000 support is in place. My red line (no upgrade while an UltraFan is in development) does not bite this round. It fails on value: -6.48 / -6.48 / -6.48 / -6.46 against its $2B bill, and -1.48 even before strain. I am for it as a time-on-wing tool [RX-0285], but the arithmetic wins. RED-LINE FLAG (CEO's company rule, not my veto): no widebody programme beside the Joint Venture unless its item value, strain counted, fits the $3B cap. The CEO must strike it. Not binding.

vetoes.plan: C: A + `ultrafan_wb: launch`
vetoes.ground: Not a Civil ground unless a date earlier than 2051 (launch + 6) is disclosed. A ready date of 2051 against a 2050 Re-engine EIS in S3 and S4 is a late engine: a Ready-by-EIS fail, as advice. Item -9.00 / -9.00 / -8.28 / -8.02 against its $4B bill. RED-LINE FLAGS (company rules, not my veto): no UltraFan WB without a 787 or A350 Re-engine on the public record [R-1574], and its value is outside the $1B sub-cap. The CEO must strike it. Not binding.

vetoes.plan: Conditional, for the final package at the veto check: a public statement or public other move that gives a Joint Venture engine date other than the bulletin's, an UltraFan WB date before 2051, or a time-on-wing target; a rationale or move that counts on an engine before its ready year; any move that shortens the inspection or test regime on the in-service Joint Venture engine to hold the ramp (compressed maturity in service, inference); or one that drops the narrowbody support plan
vetoes.ground: Civil veto grounds: compressed maturity, an early date, or no support. NOT invoked: nothing tested breaches them. If any of these appears in the final orders, statement or moves, I invoke the veto at the check and the team rule makes it binding. The grounds rest on attributed CMD turns (RX-0296, RX-0284, RX-0283).

ops.would_change_mind_if: An in-service finding on the Joint Venture engine, or on P&W's gear or GTF Advantage core modules: durability, a life-limited part or a hot-section shortfall. I would report it at once to the Board and the Safety, Energy Transition & Tech Committee and advise a fix and a slower ramp. Never a shorter inspection, and I would invoke the binding Civil veto on any move that shortened one. If the MRO and spares split for P&W's modules is not agreed jointly, I would ask for it on the Board agenda as a support gap. On widebody: in 2050 I would back the upgrade (counting from 2053), or UltraFan WB for a re-engined A350, only if a Re-engine is on the record and McCabe's break-even shows the item, with the $5B strain counted, inside the $3B cap or the $1B sub-cap. I would also back a widebody case if a column showed the 50% line at risk. Named airline wins for the Joint Venture engine on NGSA would firm up the capacity plan.
ops.memo:
Tufan, Helen, Civil's 2045 test.

In service. The Joint Venture engine was ready in 2036 on GTF2's six-year schedule and entered service on NGSA in 2037, a year in hand. Its maturity at entry rested on Pratt's test programme, not our folded UltraFan, so P&W's gear and GTF Advantage core data now come to the Committee through the Joint Venture. No in-service finding is on the record; I cite none I can't source. Nothing on the record says slow the ramp. If something does, it's a fix and a slower ramp, never a shorter inspection.

Support. Partner shops, spares, repair and the EIS team were in place by 2036. Our fleet is about 2,900 engines today and about 8,200 by 2050, 2.8 times. Partner MRO and the spare pool scale with it, and the MRO split for Pratt's modules has to be agreed jointly.

Capacity. 830 engines this year, 1,010 in 2052, five times our 188 widebody. High-performing suppliers, dual sourcing, and widebody kits and spares get first call.

Widebody. 55.2% in every column, 5.2 points above the line. I'm for the upgrade as a time-on-wing tool, but it's -1.48 before strain and -6.48 with it. UltraFan WB is ready in 2051, a year after any 2050 Re-engine, and buys no 2050 share. No Civil veto on either; hold both.

Disclosure. The draft line passes: no date. Keep 'ramp second' private; publicly it reads as Airbus's ramp.

Orders: all hold. No veto. We're keeping our engines flying and earning.

other_moves.move: In-service watch on the Joint Venture engine, P&W modules included (Board recommendation 1; Watson's condition)
other_moves.detail: Watson's maturity watch becomes an in-service watch. Each round he reports to the Board and to the Safety, Energy Transition & Tech Committee on durability, time on wing, shop-visit rates, spares cover, early-service intervention and any open findings. P&W's durability data on the gear and GTF Advantage core modules comes to the Committee through the Joint Venture each round: time on wing, life-limited parts, findings and the status of the hot-section kit. Our assurance on those modules now rests on P&W's data, because the engine took GTF2's schedule. Today the record shows no in-service finding, and we cite no in-service figure we cannot source. Rule: if an issue arises, the fleet comes first and the ramp second. The answer is a fix and a slower ramp, never a shorter inspection or test regime. Any move that shortens one triggers Watson's binding Civil veto. 'Customer trust and confidence has to be our #1 goal.'

other_moves.move: Narrowbody support plan scaled with the fleet (Watson's advice)
other_moves.detail: The support plan was in place before the 2037 EIS: partner MRO shops on the Singapore joint-venture model by 2032; repair technology, a spare-engine pool and high-performing suppliers by 2035; the EIS team and early-service intervention by 2036. The RR-delivered fleet grows from about 2,900 engines at end-2044 to about 8,200 by end-2050. Partner MRO capacity and the spare pool are sized on measured shop-visit rates as the fleet grows, not on an assumed rate. The MRO and spares split for P&W's modules, and our use of P&W's GTF shop network, are agreed jointly with P&W. If no agreement is reached, the gap goes on the Board agenda as a support item.

other_moves.move: Capacity plan for the narrowbody ramp, widebody first (Board recommendation 2)
other_moves.detail: Narrowbody engines: 830 (2045), 866 (2046), 861 (2047), 887 (2048), 925 (2049), 913 (2050), 987 (2051), peaking at 1,010 (2052), then falling to 574 by 2060. Widebody: 188 a year. Our share of the work goes to high-performing suppliers, with critical parts dual-sourced. The gear and core come only from P&W, through P&W's own chain. That concentration on one partner is flagged to the Committee. Trent kits, spares and time-on-wing engineering keep first call on engineering and supply, so 'widebody never starved' holds off the grid as well as on it. After 2052, OE capacity moves to repair and the partner-shop aftermarket; we add no owned capacity that would sit idle. The plan goes to the Committee.

other_moves.move: Trent XWB, Trent 1000 and Trent 7000 time on wing inside the existing envelope (Board recommendation 3)
other_moves.detail: The widebody core is defended without a programme and without the $5B strain: the Trent 1000 durability package, longer-life HP turbine blades and life-limited parts on the Trent 1000 and Trent 7000, and Trent XWB time on wing. No time-on-wing target goes public until its technology risk is gone. Each round we report the franchise numbers: 58.0% (2040), 55.2% (2045) and 55.2% (2050) in every column. Watch item: in S3, Airbus's widebody airframe share falls to 40.2% by 2050.

other_moves.move: Standard terms for the Joint Venture engine
other_moves.detail: Rolls-Royce offers the Joint Venture engine on standard terms, jointly with Pratt & Whitney, on NGSA and in any campaign. No launch-style discount, concession or free upgrade.

other_moves.move: Capital frame and the narrowbody bound (McCabe; Board recommendation 4)
other_moves.detail: Our narrowbody development money is final at $5.71B: the $4B Joint Venture share plus the $1.71B written off at the 2035 fold. The $4B bound is missed by $1.71B, and we state that openly. No order can change it. No further narrowbody development spend is planned, and the gross R&D envelope returns to broadly flat. Narrowbody value is engine lifecycle value: $12.6B nominal in 2045 against $5.3B under the status quo, peaking at $16.6B in 2052. It arrives as LTSA balance growth over the life of the engines, not as in-year cash, and it follows no straight line. It goes through the capital order: the balance sheet first, then the 30-40% payout, then investment and further distributions on fit, value and timing. No equity, no leverage for distributions. We guide low. Any change to medium-term guidance goes to the Board before release. An issue on P&W's modules is unpriced. A slower ramp defers value rather than losing it: about $0.75B nominal for each 10% of a year's narrowbody deliveries deferred. Any change to the Joint Venture terms, and any inducement, goes to the Board with McCabe's co-signature.

other_moves.move: Round-2 `withdraw` test retired as overtaken (to the Board)
other_moves.detail: Both partners committed in 2035 and the Joint Venture formed that round. A withdraw is available only before formation, and NGSA flies the engine, so it is not an orphan. Our narrowbody money fell from $8.0B to $5.71B. The case we feared, a formation on a finished, fully spent engine in 2045, did not happen.

other_moves.move: Forward look for 2050: widebody break-even (private, not an order)
other_moves.detail: The Joint Venture is ready and cannot be cancelled, so any widebody programme pays the $5B strain. On McCabe's break-even, a 2050 widebody case reaches the Board only under two conditions. First, a 787 or A350 Re-engine must be on the public record (for a 787 Re-engine, Boeing must have named UltraFan). Second, the Re-engine gain must be at least about $8B PV for UltraFan WB, or about $4B for the upgrade, to fit the caps. This grid's best gain is +0.98. An UltraFan WB launched in 2050 would be ready in 2056, so it cannot meet a Re-engine launched in the same round (EIS 2055). We do not expect a case.

decision.public_statement: So, our Joint Venture engine with Pratt & Whitney is in service. Our narrowbody programme folded into the Joint Venture in 2035, and that replaces our earlier line on UltraFan for the narrowbody. Our narrowbody development is complete. Our focus now is maturity and time on wing, and they come first on every fleet we power, narrowbody and Trent. We offer the engine on standard terms, jointly with our partner. Widebody is our core, and we defend it through time on wing. Frankly, we don't commit that easily. We won't do anything not profitable. I will say that categorically.
decision.rationale:
DECISION: hold on every field. That is the grid row 'UltraFan NB: hold', at +9.98 / +9.97 / +9.98 / +10.23 (S1-S4), or +9.99 expected. It is the best plan in every column, so the premium is $0. No order differs from the default, so there is no Board item.

STEP 1: START FROM MY PROPOSAL. My frame proposed all hold. Both memos recommend the same orders.

STEP 2: BINDING VETOES.
- McCabe withholds her co-signature on `t1000_upgrade: launch` and on `ultrafan_wb: launch`. Her vetoes are binding, and both orders stay `hold`.
- Her third veto, on any concession or change of Joint Venture terms, does not apply. The terms move is standard and agreed jointly with P&W.
- She sees no balance-sheet ground.
- Watson invokes no Civil veto on plan A. He passes all three tests: maturity, because the engine was ready in 2036 on GTF2's full six-year programme, a year before NGSA's 2037 EIS, so nothing was compressed; no early date, because the statement gives no date; and support, in place by 2036.
- His conditional veto (a shortened inspection regime, an early date or a dropped support plan) is not triggered. The statement and moves contain none of these, and the in-service move forbids a shorter inspection outright.
- No veto stands against the final package, so there is no revision.

STEP 3: EXPECTED SCENARIO AND BEST GRID PLAN.
Weights, confirmed by McCabe: S1 0.75, S2 0.10, S3 0.10, S4 0.05.
- S2 is low because Boeing says 'the business case isn't there yet' and gives no date. Code 5 is only one of the three codes it names.
- S3 is low because Boeing says '787 and 777X lines are stable'.
- S4 is low because Airbus is silent on an A350 Re-engine.

Expected scenario: S1. The hold row is worth +9.99 on the base set, +9.99 with S2 doubled (McCabe's guide-low set), +10.00 with S3 and S4 raised, and +10.00 on my guide-low set. No vote turns on the weights.

Item values against hold (row minus 'UltraFan NB: hold'):
- `t1000_upgrade: launch`: -6.48 / -6.48 / -6.48 / -6.46, -6.48 on every weight set. Before the $5B strain it is -1.48. The worst column is 3.24 times its $2B bill.
- `ultrafan_wb: launch`: -9.00 / -9.00 / -8.28 / -8.02, -8.88 weighted. Before the strain it is -4.00 / -4.00 / -3.28 / -3.02. The worst column is 2.25 times its $4B bill.

Neither fits the premium caps ($3B, and $1B for UltraFan WB), and both lose more than their own bill in every column. Struck on value.

STEP 4: DOCTRINE AGAINST RECORD. My record favours the Trent 1000 upgrade: 'regain market share? Absolutely' [RX-0101] and 'Why not?' [RX-0117]. My profile keeps it only as a declared premium within $3B. At $6.48B it is far outside that, and it fails before the strain too: it buys 4.8 pp of widebody share at about $1.35B a point while the core already sits 5.2 pp above the line. The arithmetic wins. On UltraFan WB, the 'airframers first' test [RX-0058] fails outright: no Re-engine is on the record and Boeing has named nothing. It also buys no 2050 share, because it is ready in 2051, a year after a 2050 Re-engine EIS in S3 and S4. The four-part gate [RX-0030] fails on market and business model for both items.

STEP 5: RED-LINE FLAGS.
- Watson flagged B (the upgrade beside the Joint Venture outside the cap) and C (UltraFan WB with no Re-engine on the record, and outside the $1B sub-cap).
- McCabe flagged C (no programme that can fly it).
- I confirm all three. Both items are struck and neither is ordered. No flag stands against the final package.
- Other red lines in force are met:
  - Safety first: fleet first, ramp second, never a shorter inspection.
  - No disclosed date.
  - No concessions.
  - No options management: the formed Joint Venture stays because NGSA flies it.
  - No equity and no leverage for distributions.
  - `overrides` is empty.

STEP 6: SITUATION AND CASH. The narrowbody entry is built, selected, ready and in service. Narrowbody money is final at $5.71B. It misses the $4B bound by $1.71B, and we say so openly; no order can change it. With the Joint Venture ready and impossible to cancel, any widebody programme carries a $5B strain for the rest of the game. That strain is charged only if a widebody programme is added, so it belongs in the item value. The cash question this round is therefore not a launch: it is maturity, time on wing, capacity and capital order. Tomorrow's financials [RX-0125] come from a mature narrowbody fleet and a widebody fleet that stays on wing.

STEP 7: TIE-BREAK. Not needed. All three of us agree.

DISCLOSURE. The out-of-date 'in development ... no earlier than 2037' line is replaced. I take Watson's advice: 'fleet first, ramp second' stays a private rule, because in public it could be read as a comment on Airbus's ramp or as a hint of a finding. The public wording is 'maturity and time on wing come first, on every fleet we power'. The statement gives no date, no engine choice for any airframer, nothing on Airbus's ramp, nothing on P&W's modules and no widebody programme.

THIN-RECORD NOTE. My record has no evidence on in-service partner modules or Joint Venture MRO splits. On those I defer to Watson. On the value of the narrowbody cash and the capital frame I take McCabe's test as my evidence (profile fallback).

It goes through the capital order: the balance sheet first, then the 30-40% payout, then investment and further distributions on fit, value and timing. No equity, no leverage for distributions. We guide low. Any change to medium-term guidance goes to the Board before release. An issue on P&W's modules is unpriced. A slower ramp defers value rather than losing it: about $0.75B nominal for each 10% of a year's narrowbody deliveries deferred. Any change to the Joint Venture terms, and any inducement, goes to the Board with McCabe's co-signature.

other_moves.move: Round-2 `withdraw` test retired as overtaken (to the Board)
other_moves.detail: Both partners committed in 2035 and the Joint Venture formed that round. A withdraw is available only before formation, and NGSA flies the engine, so it is not an orphan. Our narrowbody money fell from $8.0B to $5.71B. The case we feared, a formation on a finished, fully spent engine in 2045, did not happen.

other_moves.move: Forward look for 2050: widebody break-even (private, not an order)
other_moves.detail: The Joint Venture is ready and cannot be cancelled, so any widebody programme pays the $5B strain. On McCabe's break-even, a 2050 widebody case reaches the Board only under two conditions. First, a 787 or A350 Re-engine must be on the public record (for a 787 Re-engine, Boeing must have named UltraFan). Second, the Re-engine gain must be at least about $8B PV for UltraFan WB, or about $4B for the upgrade, to fit the caps. This grid's best gain is +0.98. An UltraFan WB launched in 2050 would be ready in 2056, so it cannot meet a Re-engine launched in the same round (EIS 2055). We do not expect a case.

final.public_statement: So, our Joint Venture engine with Pratt & Whitney is in service. Our narrowbody programme folded into the Joint Venture in 2035, and that replaces our earlier line on UltraFan for the narrowbody. Our narrowbody development is complete. Our focus now is maturity and time on wing, and they come first on every fleet we power, narrowbody and Trent. We offer the engine on standard terms, jointly with our partner. Widebody is our core, and we defend it through time on wing. Frankly, we don't commit that easily. We won't do anything not profitable. I will say that categorically.
final.rationale:
DECISION: hold on every field. That is the grid row 'UltraFan NB: hold', at +9.98 / +9.97 / +9.98 / +10.23 (S1-S4), or +9.99 expected. It is the best plan in every column, so the premium is $0. No order differs from the default, so there is no Board item.

STEP 1: START FROM MY PROPOSAL. My frame proposed all hold. Both memos recommend the same orders.

STEP 2: BINDING VETOES.
- McCabe withholds her co-signature on `t1000_upgrade: launch` and on `ultrafan_wb: launch`. Her vetoes are binding, and both orders stay `hold`.
- Her third veto, on any concession or change of Joint Venture terms, does not apply. The terms move is standard and agreed jointly with P&W.
- She sees no balance-sheet ground.
- Watson invokes no Civil veto on plan A. He passes all three tests: maturity, because the engine was ready in 2036 on GTF2's full six-year programme, a year before NGSA's 2037 EIS, so nothing was compressed; no early date, because the statement gives no date; and support, in place by 2036.
- His conditional veto (a shortened inspection regime, an early date or a dropped support plan) is not triggered. The statement and moves contain none of these, and the in-service move forbids a shorter inspection outright.
- No veto stands against the final package, so there is no revision.

STEP 3: EXPECTED SCENARIO AND BEST GRID PLAN.
Weights, confirmed by McCabe: S1 0.75, S2 0.10, S3 0.10, S4 0.05.
- S2 is low because Boeing says 'the business case isn't there yet' and gives no date. Code 5 is only one of the three codes it names.
- S3 is low because Boeing says '787 and 777X lines are stable'.
- S4 is low because Airbus is silent on an A350 Re-engine.

Expected scenario: S1. The hold row is worth +9.99 on the base set, +9.99 with S2 doubled (McCabe's guide-low set), +10.00 with S3 and S4 raised, and +10.00 on my guide-low set. No vote turns on the weights.

Item values against hold (row minus 'UltraFan NB: hold'):
- `t1000_upgrade: launch`: -6.48 / -6.48 / -6.48 / -6.46, -6.48 on every weight set. Before the $5B strain it is -1.48. The worst column is 3.24 times its $2B bill.
- `ultrafan_wb: launch`: -9.00 / -9.00 / -8.28 / -8.02, -8.88 weighted. Before the strain it is -4.00 / -4.00 / -3.28 / -3.02. The worst column is 2.25 times its $4B bill.

Neither fits the premium caps ($3B, and $1B for UltraFan WB), and both lose more than their own bill in every column. Struck on value.

STEP 4: DOCTRINE AGAINST RECORD. My record favours the Trent 1000 upgrade: 'regain market share? Absolutely' [RX-0101] and 'Why not?' [RX-0117]. My profile keeps it only as a declared premium within $3B. At $6.48B it is far outside that, and it fails before the strain too: it buys 4.8 pp of widebody share at about $1.35B a point while the core already sits 5.2 pp above the line. The arithmetic wins. On UltraFan WB, the 'airframers first' test [RX-0058] fails outright: no Re-engine is on the record and Boeing has named nothing. It also buys no 2050 share, because it is ready in 2051, a year after a 2050 Re-engine EIS in S3 and S4. The four-part gate [RX-0030] fails on market and business model for both items.

STEP 5: RED-LINE FLAGS.
- Watson flagged B (the upgrade beside the Joint Venture outside the cap) and C (UltraFan WB with no Re-engine on the record, and outside the $1B sub-cap).
- McCabe flagged C (no programme that can fly it).
- I confirm all three. Both items are struck and neither is ordered. No flag stands against the final package.
- Other red lines in force are met:
  - Safety first: fleet first, ramp second, never a shorter inspection.
  - No disclosed date.
  - No concessions.
  - No options management: the formed Joint Venture stays because NGSA flies it.
  - No equity and no leverage for distributions.
  - `overrides` is empty.

STEP 6: SITUATION AND CASH. The narrowbody entry is built, selected, ready and in service. Narrowbody money is final at $5.71B. It misses the $4B bound by $1.71B, and we say so openly; no order can change it. With the Joint Venture ready and impossible to cancel, any widebody programme carries a $5B strain for the rest of the game. That strain is charged only if a widebody programme is added, so it belongs in the item value. The cash question this round is therefore not a launch: it is maturity, time on wing, capacity and capital order. Tomorrow's financials [RX-0125] come from a mature narrowbody fleet and a widebody fleet that stays on wing.

STEP 7: TIE-BREAK. Not needed. All three of us agree.

DISCLOSURE. The out-of-date 'in development ... no earlier than 2037' line is replaced. I take Watson's advice: 'fleet first, ramp second' stays a private rule, because in public it could be read as a comment on Airbus's ramp or as a hint of a finding. The public wording is 'maturity and time on wing come first, on every fleet we power'. The statement gives no date, no engine choice for any airframer, nothing on Airbus's ramp, nothing on P&W's modules and no widebody programme.

THIN-RECORD NOTE. My record has no evidence on in-service partner modules or Joint Venture MRO splits. On those I defer to Watson. On the value of the narrowbody cash and the capital frame I take McCabe's test as my evidence (profile fallback).

memo_weighing.cfo:
Taken in full, and binding where she made it so.
- She confirms my weights (S1 0.75, S2 0.10, S3 0.10, S4 0.05) and every grid figure.
- She withholds her co-signature on both widebody launches. I respect both vetoes; they match my lean, so nothing needed revising.

- Her capital frame goes into the moves as written: lifecycle value as LTSA growth, a peak of $16.6B in 2052, no straight lines, guide low.
- The P&W-module risk is unpriced; a slower ramp defers value rather than losing it. Taken as written.
- Her 2050 break-even (about $8B for UltraFan WB, about $4B for the upgrade) frames the last round.
- She marks the `withdraw` test as overtaken. Agreed.
- Her red-line flag on UltraFan WB is confirmed and the item is struck.
memo_weighing.ops:
Taken in full.
- No Civil veto on all-hold. The engine was ready in 2036 on GTF2's full programme, not on compressed maturity, so there is no early date, and support was in place by 2036.
- His note that maturity assurance on the core and gear now comes through P&W's data became a condition: P&W module data goes to the Committee each round.

final.objective_note:
- Enter the narrowbody market: met. 25.2% in 2045, 27.2% in 2050.
- Keep widebody dominance: met. 58.0% in 2040, 55.2% in 2045 and 2050 in every column, 5.2 pp above the line.
- Bounded narrowbody risk: NOT met. Final at $5.71B ($4B Joint Venture share plus $1.71B fold write-off), $1.71B over the $4B bound, stated openly. No order can change it, and no further narrowbody development spend is planned.
- Widebody never starved: met, with the strain at $0, but only while every widebody field holds. Any upgrade or UltraFan WB would now charge $5B for the rest of the game.
final.predictions:
Base case S1 (0.75).
- Boeing does not launch the fps this round; the business case is not there.
- No 787 or A350 Re-engine.
- NGSA keeps CFM + PW + RR.
- CFM's ducted engine and the Embraer partnership keep counting. RISE stays a technology programme until an airframer launches with it.
- P&W keeps GTF fleet work first and stays on standard terms in the Joint Venture.

Our position at hold:
- Narrowbody share 25.2% (2045) and 27.2% (2050); widebody 55.2%; strain $0.
- ΔPV +9.98 (S1), +9.97 (S2), +9.98 (S3), +10.23 (S4); +9.99 expected.

Risks:
- S2 (0.10): an fps on code 5 is worth -0.01 against S1, so no concession could pay.
- S3 (0.10): Airbus's widebody airframe share falls to 40.2% by 2050; our engine share is unchanged on this board.
- S4 (0.05): the best column, +10.23.
- An in-service finding on the P&W modules is unpriced. It would slow the ramp, deferring value rather than losing it.

For 2050 I expect to hold again. A widebody case would need a Re-engine on the record and a gain of about $8B (UltraFan WB) or $4B (upgrade), and I do not expect one.

board_response.recommendation: R1 (2045): in-service maturity and support of the Joint Venture engine, reported each round to the Board and the Committee; fleet first, ramp second; never a shorter inspection.
board_response.response: Taken up (other move 1). Watson reports each round, and P&W's data on the gear and GTF Advantage core comes to the Committee through the Joint Venture. His note matters here: the engine took GTF2's six-year schedule, so our assurance on those modules rests on P&W's data. Today the record shows no in-service finding, and we cite no in-service figure we cannot source. If an issue arises, the answer is a fix and a slower ramp, never a shorter inspection or test regime. A move that shortened one would trigger Watson's binding Civil veto. Customer trust first.

board_response.recommendation: R2 (2045): capacity for the narrowbody ramp without starving the widebody core.
board_response.response:
Taken up (moves 2 and 3).
- Volumes: 830 narrowbody engines in 2045, rising to 1,010 in 2052, then down to 574 by 2060, against 188 widebody a year.
- Our share of the work goes to high-performing suppliers, with critical parts dual-sourced.
- Partner MRO on the Singapore model works together with P&W's shop network, with the MRO and spares split for P&W modules agreed jointly.
- Trent kits, spares and time-on-wing engineering keep first call.
- Our dependence on P&W alone for the gear and core is flagged.
- After 2052, OE capacity moves to repair; we add no owned capacity that would sit idle.
- The plan goes to the Committee.

board_response.recommendation: R3 (2045): hold both widebody fields; defend the core through time on wing; bring a 2050 case only with a Re-engine on the record and the strain counted within the caps; watch S3; report franchise numbers.
board_response.response: Taken up. Both fields hold: the upgrade is -6.48 and UltraFan WB -8.88 against hold, each below its own bill in every column, and McCabe withheld her co-signature on both. Widebody share is 58.0% / 55.2% / 55.2% in every column. Time-on-wing work continues inside the envelope (move 4). The S3 watch (40.2%) is noted. For 2050, a case needs a Re-engine on the record and, on McCabe's break-even, a gain of about $8B (UltraFan WB) or $4B (upgrade). An UltraFan WB launched in 2050 cannot meet a same-round Re-engine. We do not expect a case.

board_response.recommendation: R4 (2045): capital frame and the narrowbody bound stated openly.
board_response.response: Taken up (move 6). Narrowbody money is final at $5.71B: the $4B Joint Venture share plus the $1.71B fold write-off. The bound is missed by $1.71B, stated openly. No further narrowbody development spend; the gross R&D envelope returns to broadly flat. Narrowbody value goes through the capital order: balance sheet, the 30-40% payout, then investment and distributions on fit, value and timing. It is LTSA growth, not in-year cash, peaking around 2052. No equity and no leverage for distributions. We guide low, and any guidance change comes to the Board before release.

board_response.recommendation: R5 (2045): Joint Venture terms and commercial discipline; answer the round-2 `withdraw` test as overtaken.
board_response.response: Taken up. The `withdraw` test is overtaken: both partners committed in 2035, the Joint Venture formed, our narrowbody money fell from $8.0B to $5.71B, and NGSA flies the engine (move 7). The engine is offered only on standard terms, jointly with P&W (move 5, public). An fps selection is worth -0.01, so no concession can pay. Any change of terms or any inducement comes to the Board with McCabe's co-signature.

board_response.recommendation: R6 (2045): disclosure. Replace the out-of-date line; no airframer dates or engine choices; no widebody programme; 'We won't do anything not profitable' stands.
board_response.response: Taken up. The 'in development ... no earlier than 2037' line is replaced, and the statement says the Joint Venture engine is in service with the focus on maturity and time on wing. On Watson's advice, 'fleet first, ramp second' stays a private rule so it cannot be read as a comment on Airbus's ramp. The statement gives no date, no engine choice for any airframer, nothing on P&W's modules and no widebody programme, and the 'not profitable' line stands.

board_response.recommendation: Round-2 recommendation: the 2045 exit for the standing commitment (bring `withdraw` against keeping the commit).
board_response.response: Overtaken. Both partners committed in 2035 and the Joint Venture formed that round, so no withdraw is available. The feared case, a formation on a fully spent engine in 2045 with shares equalised for nothing, did not happen. The grid booked the saving: narrowbody money is $5.71B, not $8.0B.

board_response.recommendation: Round-2 recommendation: the maturity watch and integration plan (the folded UltraFan's test schedule governs).
board_response.response: Answered and carried forward. The engine took GTF2's schedule, the one further along, not the folded UltraFan's. Watson finds the 2036 ready date earned on P&W's full six-year programme, so maturity was not compressed. The watch is now an in-service watch, with P&W's module data coming to the Committee through the Joint Venture.

board_response.recommendation: Round-2 recommendations on disclosure, terms, capital frame and the widebody core.
board_response.response:
Met.
- Disclosure: no Joint Venture date has been given, and none is given now.
- Terms: standard terms held, with no concession.
- Capital frame: reported as final at $5.71B.
- Widebody core: no widebody programme, because no Re-engine reached the record. Share stays at 55.2%, with time on wing inside the envelope.
